procedures: Before applying, the Administrator obtains or draws a floor plan of every level. The plan shows all internal and external exits, room numbers, square footage of each living unit, bathrooms, common areas, fire-safe areas and exit paths. It is dated and signed.

The Administrator measures each living unit and records its square footage on the Living Unit Schedule. The schedule marks whether the unit is existing construction or new construction after 1/18/2011. A single unit is 225 sq ft or more in new construction or 160 sq ft or more in existing construction.
The Administrator sets the maximum occupancy of each unit at 1 or 2. A unit is used as shared only when both residents have agreed in writing, and the agreement is kept in each resident's record.

Before opening, the Maintenance Lead [NAME/TITLE] checks every unit for a lockable door with a master key held by designated staff, a phone jack, a thermostat and an emergency notification system. Any deficiency is fixed and the date recorded before the unit is occupied.
The Administrator confirms that each floor has two independent exits and that egress routes are unlocked and unobstructed. The Maintenance Lead walks all egress routes weekly and logs the check.
The Administrator posts emergency procedures in common areas. If the licensed capacity is 9 or more residents, the Administrator also posts floor diagrams showing exits and routes.

The Administrator identifies any resident with a mobility need who lives above or below grade and confirms that a fire-safe area is available. Placement is recorded in the evacuation plan (see SAF-04).
The Administrator notifies the local fire department in writing of the residence's location, capacity and use. A copy of the letter is kept in the licensing binder.

The Administrator obtains written fire safety approval before licensure. The Administrator calendars the renewal date so that approval is renewed at least every 3 years, with a reminder at 6 months before it lapses.

If fire safety approval is withdrawn or restricted, the Administrator notifies DHS orally at once and in writing within 48 hours. The Administrator also reviews placement with the licensing office on the same business day.
After any renovation, the Administrator submits new fire safety approval to DHS within 15 days. Renovated areas are not occupied until the Administrator has confirmed that the approvals are in place.

If the building has an elevator, the Administrator keeps the current Elevator Certificate with the floor plan. If the residence has or seeks a special care designation, the Administrator assembles the environmental or physical-site evidence and refers to SCU-01.
The Administrator tracks the census daily against licensed capacity. No admission is made if it would exceed licensed capacity.
To raise capacity, the Administrator submits a written request to DHS and other required authorities. No additional resident is admitted until written approval is received.

Before the DHS inspection, DHS inspects before initial licensure and reinspects within 3 months. The Administrator checks the floor plan, living unit schedule, fire safety approval and posted items against the building and corrects any difference.

The Administrator pays the license fees DHS bills. The base is $300 plus $75 per bed, adjusted by DHS for CPI. The special care designation fee is $150. The Administrator confirms the current amounts with DHS before sending payment. The term 'assisted living' is used in advertising only after the residence is licensed.
The Administrator reviews the floor plan and capacity items every year at licensure renewal and after any change. A new dated copy replaces the old one in the licensing binder.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps the floor plan, living unit schedule, capacity record and fire approval current. Submits notices and requests to DHS and the fire authorities.
Inspects doors, keys, thermostats, phone jacks, emergency notification systems and egress routes and logs results.
Check census against licensed capacity and the living unit schedule before every admission and every room change.
Approves capital changes and renovations only after the Administrator has confirmed the DHS and fire approval steps.

documentation: Dated floor plan of every level with all exits
Elevator Certificate (if applicable)
SCU environmental or physical-site evidence (if applicable)
Living Unit Schedule with square footage and occupancy
Written fire safety approval and renewal calendar
Written notice to the local fire department
Records of DHS capacity approvals
Weekly egress and unit check logs
Shared-unit written agreements

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Reportable Incidents and Conditions Policy
policies.applies_to: ALR and PCH; all staff, volunteers and contractors
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents and conditions that affect resident health, safety or rights are prevented where possible, reported on time to DHS, the resident's family and the designated person, investigated and documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets application checklist item 8(a), Reportable Incidents and Conditions Policy (§ 2600.16(b)). For an assisted living residence, it also meets 55 Pa. Code §2800.16(b), which requires written prevention, reporting and investigation policies for the 20 reportable incidents or conditions. These include death, an injury requiring hospital-level care, a rights violation, an unexplained absence, misuse of resident funds, an outbreak of illness, a fire, a medication error and termination of a utility. [AGENCY NAME] keeps the full DHS list of 20 incidents and conditions in the Reportable Incident Matrix and trains staff on it. Under §2800.16(c)-(f), the Administrator reports each reportable incident or condition to the DHS ALR office or hotline within 24 hours. The family and the designated person are told immediately. After the investigation, the Administrator submits a final report on the DHS form. If the incident is validated, affected residents are informed. A copy of each report is kept. Staff must tell the Administrator about any possible reportable incident immediately. No staff person may delay or discourage a report, and retaliation against anyone who reports is prohibited.

definitions.definition: An event or situation on the DHS list of 20 items in §2800.16(b), such as death, a hospital-level injury, a rights violation, an unexplained absence, fund misuse, an outbreak, a fire, a medication error or loss of a utility.
The person a resident has named in writing to be notified and to act on the resident's behalf for notices.
The written report on the DHS incident form submitted after the investigation is complete.
The residence's one-page list of all 20 DHS reportable items with examples, used for staff training and shift checks.

procedures: Any staff person who sees, hears of or suspects an incident or condition on the Incident Matrix tells the supervisor on duty immediately, and tells the Administrator by phone at [PHONE] the same shift.
The staff person gives first aid, calls 911 if there is danger to life, and makes the resident safe before starting any paperwork (see POL-12).
The supervisor starts an Incident Report that day. It states the date, time, place, residents and staff involved, what happened, witnesses, actions taken and who was notified.
The Administrator decides within 1 hour of being told whether the event is reportable. If there is doubt, it is treated as reportable.

The Administrator reports the incident to the DHS ALR office or hotline at [DHS REGIONAL ALR OFFICE / HOTLINE NUMBER] within 24 hours, and records the date, time, person spoken to and any reference given.

The Administrator or a designee notifies the resident's family and designated person immediately, and records who was told, the time and the method. If no one can be reached, the attempts are logged and repeated.

For suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator follows the added reporting steps in SAF-01 at the same time. For a death, an unexplained absence or an outbreak, the Administrator also follows HC-02, SAF-03 and SAF-05.
The Administrator starts an investigation the same day. It includes interviews with staff, the resident and witnesses, a review of records and logs, and a check of the scene.
Staff involved in the incident are interviewed separately and are removed from contact with the affected resident if the Administrator thinks that is needed to protect residents.

The Administrator decides whether the allegation or condition is validated and writes the finding with reasons. The Administrator then lists corrective actions, with responsible persons and due dates.
The Administrator submits the final report on the DHS form after the investigation is complete, and keeps a copy with the incident file.
If the incident is validated, the Administrator informs the affected residents (and their designated persons) of the finding and of the corrective action, and records the date and who was told.
The Administrator reviews each resident's support plan after any incident that affects care and updates it if needed (see FRM-03).
Incident files are kept in a locked file with limited access, consistent with POL-02 and POL-17.
The Administrator keeps an Incident Log listing every report by date, type, DHS report date and time, family notice date and time, final report date and corrective action status.

Each quarter the Administrator presents the Incident Log trends to the Quality Management review (POL-03). Staff are trained on this policy and on the Incident Matrix at orientation and every year (see PLAN-01).

responsibilities.duty: Decides reportability, reports to DHS within 24 hours, notifies family and designated person, completes the investigation and final report, and keeps copies.
Secures resident safety, starts the Incident Report and informs the Administrator immediately.
Report any possible incident at once and cooperate with the investigation.
Reviews quarterly incident trends and supports corrective action.

documentation: Incident Report forms
Reportable Incident Matrix (20 items)
Incident Log
Record of DHS report (date, time, person, reference)
Record of family and designated person notices
Investigation notes and findings
Final report on the DHS form (copy)
Record of notice to affected residents when validated
Staff training records on this policy

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Confidentiality and Privacy Policy
policies.applies_to: ALR and PCH; all staff, volunteers, contractors and visitors who may see resident information
policies.purpose: To protect resident records and personal information, to limit who may see them, and to state the written consent rules and the exceptions allowed by law.
policies.policy: This policy meets application checklist item 8(b), Confidentiality Policy (§ 2600.17). For an assisted living residence, it also meets 55 Pa. Code §2800.17. Resident records are confidential. Without the resident's written consent, only the resident, the designated person, staff who provide services to the resident, authorized DHS agents and the ombudsman may see them. The exceptions are an emergency and a court order. Records are kept locked under the record security procedures in POL-17. If [AGENCY NAME] is a covered entity under HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), it also follows those rules, and the Administrator will determine and document that status. Staff may share resident information only as needed to carry out their duties. Breaches of this policy are cause for discipline up to termination.

definitions.definition: All written or electronic information about a resident, including the medical evaluation, assessment, support plan, medication records, incident reports and financial records.
A signed and dated authorization by the resident or the resident's legal representative that names the person or agency that may see the record and the information to be shared.
The person the resident has named to receive information and notices.
The long-term care ombudsman, who may see records as allowed by law.

procedures: At orientation and every year, each staff person, volunteer and contractor with access to records signs a Confidentiality Acknowledgment after training on this policy.
The Administrator keeps a written list of staff roles that may access resident records. Access is limited to what each role needs to do its work.
Paper records are kept in locked cabinets or a locked room. Only the Administrator and staff on the access list hold keys or codes.
Electronic records require unique user names and passwords. Screens are locked when staff leave a workstation, and passwords are not shared.
Staff do not discuss residents in public areas, on personal social media or with visitors. Resident names are not placed in view of visitors, for example on open whiteboards.
When a request is made for a record, the Administrator confirms who is asking and why before releasing anything.
Requests from the resident, the designated person, DHS agents and the ombudsman are handled by the Administrator on the same business day, and the person's identity or authority is confirmed.

For any other person or agency, including family not named as designated person, insurers and other providers, the Administrator obtains the resident's written consent first. The consent is filed in the resident's record.
In an emergency, staff may share needed health information with emergency responders and treating providers, and the Administrator documents what was shared, with whom and when, on the same day.
On receipt of a court order, the Administrator verifies the order, releases only what the order requires and records the release. The Administrator may seek legal advice first.
The Administrator keeps a Record Disclosure Log that shows date, record or information released, recipient, basis for release (consent, DHS, ombudsman, emergency or court order) and who released it.
Photographs, video and recordings of residents need the resident's written consent. See POL-06 for voice-controlled devices and location tracking disclosures.
Faxes, emails and text messages containing resident information are sent only by secure methods, with the recipient confirmed first.

Any suspected breach, such as lost records or access by an unauthorized person, is reported to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator investigates, takes corrective action and tells the resident and designated person when information was disclosed improperly.
Records are kept and destroyed as required by POL-17. Shredding is done on site or by a contractor that gives a certificate of destruction.
The Administrator reviews confidentiality compliance each quarter as part of quality management (POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Manages access, approves releases, keeps the disclosure log and investigates breaches.
Protect resident information, share it only as needed for their work and report breaches.
Maintains locked storage and the access list.

documentation: Signed Confidentiality Acknowledgments
Access list by role
Written consents for release
Record Disclosure Log
Breach reports and corrective action
Training records on confidentiality

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Quality Management Plan
policies.applies_to: ALR and PCH; administration, all departments and the governing body
policies.purpose: To set up a written process for finding problems in the residence, correcting them and checking that the corrections worked, so that resident care and safety improve over time.
policies.policy: This policy meets application checklist item 8(c), Quality Management Plan (§ 2600.26(a)-(c)). For an assisted living residence, it also meets 55 Pa. Code §2800.26. [AGENCY NAME] has a written quality management plan that is carried out, not just kept on file. The plan periodically reviews incident reports, complaints, staff training, violations and plans of correction, and resident councils. It also puts improvement measures into action. [AGENCY NAME] sets its own review schedule at least quarterly. Each review is documented with minutes showing the date, the people present, the findings and the actions assigned, so an inspector can see that the plan is in use.

definitions.definition: A regular process of reviewing data and results, finding problems and trends, and acting to improve care.
A specific action with an owner and a due date that is meant to fix a problem found in the review.
The written response to a DHS inspection citation that says how and when a violation will be fixed.
The group that conducts the review: the Administrator, the nurse or care lead, a direct care staff person and, as available, the owner or governing body representative.

procedures: The Administrator names the Quality Management Committee [MEMBERS], with at least the Administrator, a direct care staff representative and a governing body or owner representative. The members are listed in the plan.
The Committee meets at least quarterly, on dates set in advance for the year, and meets sooner after a serious incident or a DHS citation.
Before each meeting, the Administrator compiles the Incident Log and reportable incident trends from POL-01, including medication errors, falls, injuries, outbreaks and unexplained absences.
The Administrator compiles the Complaint Log from POL-07 and notes each complaint's topic, date, resolution and time to resolve.
The Administrator compiles staff training results from PLAN-01: percent complete, overdue items and competency test results.
The Administrator compiles all DHS inspection violations, plans of correction and the status of each corrective step.
The Administrator gathers input from resident councils or resident meetings, including concerns raised, and how each was answered.
At the meeting, the Committee reviews each data set, looks for patterns by time, place, staff, shift or resident, and lists the problems found.
For each problem, the Committee decides on an improvement measure, names a responsible person and sets a due date. The decisions are written in the meeting minutes.

The Administrator puts the improvement measures into action. Examples are retraining staff, changing a procedure, repairing the building or adjusting staffing. The Administrator tells affected staff of any change within 5 business days.
At the next meeting the Committee checks whether each measure was completed and whether the problem got better. Items that have not improved are reassigned with a new plan.
The Administrator signs and dates the minutes and keeps them, along with the data summaries, in the Quality Management binder.
The Administrator provides the minutes to inspectors on request.
Once a year, the Committee reviews the whole plan for effectiveness and updates it. The revised plan is signed and dated, and staff are told of any changes.
Confidential resident information in the review materials is handled under POL-02. Review documents show resident initials or an identifier rather than full names where possible.

responsibilities.duty: Leads the Committee, compiles data, records minutes and assures improvement measures are carried out.
Reviews the data, decides on measures, tracks them to completion and reviews the plan yearly.
Provides resources for approved measures and receives the quarterly report.
Provide information and carry out assigned improvement measures by the due date.

documentation: Written Quality Management Plan
Committee member list
Dated quarterly review minutes
Data summaries (incidents, complaints, training, violations and plans of correction, resident councils)
Improvement measure tracking sheet
Annual plan review

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Accepted Forms of Payment: SSI, Private Pay and Third-Party Payers
policies.applies_to: ALR and PCH; admissions, billing and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To state which forms of payment [AGENCY NAME] accepts, to protect residents who receive SSI, to keep payer arrangements honest and clear, and to avoid promising funding that is not available.
policies.policy: This policy meets application checklist item 8(d), accepted forms of payment, including acceptance of Supplemental Security Income (SSI), private pay, and third-party payment through any Medicaid or Medicare funded program such as the Living Independence for the Elderly (LIFE) program, In Lieu of Services (ILOS), Resident Habilitation, or other sources not listed (§ 2600.27(a), (b), (c), (d)). For an assisted living residence, it also meets 55 Pa. Code §2800.27. [AGENCY NAME] accepts SSI, private pay and third-party payment. Residence charges are mostly private pay. Community HealthChoices (Medicaid long-term services and supports) generally does not pay PCH or ALR residence charges, so staff must never tell an applicant or family that it will. Charges for an SSI-eligible resident may not exceed the resident's monthly income minus the personal needs allowance. For SSI residents, hygiene items, laundry, and help with activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living are provided at no extra charge. Third-party payments may not be used for food, clothing or shelter. Fees, refund terms and bed-hold charges are written in the resident-residence contract (§2800.25). When [AGENCY NAME] handles resident funds, it follows §2800.20. Admission of any applicant, whatever the payer, remains subject to licensed capacity and to the residence's ability to meet the applicant's needs (see AR-01).

definitions.definition: Supplemental Security Income, a federal benefit, which may carry a Pennsylvania state supplement.
The portion of an SSI resident's monthly income that the resident keeps for personal use and that may not be charged by the residence.
Payment of residence charges by the resident or the resident's family or representative from personal funds.
A program or person other than the resident that pays for some services, such as LIFE, ILOS, resident habilitation or another source.
Pennsylvania's Medicaid managed long-term services and supports program. It generally does not cover PCH or ALR residence charges.

procedures: At the first inquiry, admissions staff give the applicant the fee schedule and say which payment types are accepted: private pay, SSI and third-party payers.
Admissions staff ask each applicant how the residence charges will be paid and record the answer on the Pre-Admission Screening (AR-01).

If the applicant asks about Community HealthChoices or other Medicaid, staff say that it generally does not pay PCH or ALR residence charges. Staff do not promise coverage and refer the applicant to the Area Agency on Aging or to the resident's service coordinator for questions about services.

For an SSI-eligible applicant, the Administrator obtains the current SSI award letter and confirms the monthly income. The Administrator then calculates the maximum monthly charge: monthly income minus the personal needs allowance of [CURRENT PERSONAL NEEDS ALLOWANCE AMOUNT].
The Administrator writes the SSI charge in the contract and makes sure it does not exceed that maximum. The calculation is signed and kept in the billing file.

For SSI residents, staff provide hygiene items, laundry and help with activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living at no extra charge. The contract states this, and the billing office does not add separate fees.

The Administrator checks every third-party payment arrangement, such as LIFE, ILOS or resident habilitation, in writing before admission. The Administrator confirms which services the program pays for and in what amount, and records it in the contract or an addendum.
Third-party payments are not applied to food, clothing or shelter. The billing office posts them only against the services they are authorized to cover.

Each contract includes the fee schedule, refund terms and bed-hold charges. The contract is month-to-month. The resident gives 14 days' notice and the residence gives 30 days' notice. The resident has a 72-hour right to rescind, and no life-care or asset assignment is required (see FRM-01).
The Administrator does not require, and staff do not ask for, assignment of an applicant's assets as a condition of admission.

If [AGENCY NAME] holds or manages a resident's funds, it keeps transaction records, disburses funds within 24 hours of a request, gets written receipts, and never mixes resident funds with the residence's funds. If more than $200 is held for more than 2 months, the Administrator offers the resident an interest-bearing account. Staff never hold power of attorney or guardianship for a resident. The resident gets an itemized quarterly account (see RR-01).
Billing staff issue a monthly statement showing charges, payments and any third-party amounts, and explain any change in charges in writing at least 30 days ahead, as the contract provides.

If a resident's payer changes, for example when a private-pay resident becomes SSI-eligible or funds run out, the Administrator meets with the resident or representative within 5 business days, reviews options in writing and follows the contract and POL-16 for any needed change.
The Administrator reviews payer mix and billing complaints quarterly through quality management (POL-03). Staff are trained on this policy at orientation.

responsibilities.duty: Approves payer arrangements, calculates and signs SSI charge limits, and confirms that third-party funds are used only as allowed.
Explain accepted forms of payment accurately and do not promise Community HealthChoices or other coverage.
Bill within the contract and this policy, keep resident fund records and issue statements and quarterly accounts.
Sets the fee schedule and approves any change in accepted payers.

documentation: Fee schedule
Pre-Admission Screening payer section
SSI award letter and maximum-charge calculation
Contract with fee schedule, refund terms and bed-hold charges
Third-party payer agreements or addenda
Resident fund ledgers, receipts and itemized quarterly accounts (if funds are handled)
Monthly statements
Written notices of charge changes

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Resident Rights, Notification and Rights Poster
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all residents, designated persons, staff, volunteers and contractors
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident knows, receives and can use his or her rights, and that no one at [AGENCY NAME] takes those rights away, conditions them on behavior, or retaliates against a resident who uses them.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] respects and protects the rights of every resident. This policy meets official checklist item 8(e), Resident Rights (55 Pa. Code §2600.41(a); ALR counterpart §2800.41), and item 10(b), the home's forms for the Resident Rights Poster (55 Pa. Code §2600.41; ALR counterpart §2800.41).

At admission, [AGENCY NAME] informs each resident and his or her designated person of the resident's rights and of the right to complain without retaliation. We do this in a language and mode of communication the person understands. We give each resident a copy of the rights, keep a signed acknowledgment in the resident record, and post the DHS rights poster where residents and visitors can see it.

Resident rights include, at a minimum: non-discrimination; freedom from abuse and restraints; 30 days' written notice of new rules; private use of the telephone and private mail; access to the long-term care ombudsman; visitors at any time; privacy; access to one's own records; choice of physician; and assistance with relocation (§2800.42). A resident may not be deprived of any right. Rights are never used as a reward or a sanction, and any purported waiver of a right is void (§2800.43). The residence gives immediate access to the residence, residents and records to DHS agents, the area agency on aging, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and the protection and advocacy (P&A) system. It does the same for a designated person if the resident asks, and gives community and legal-services groups access during visiting hours (§2800.5). We apply this policy without discrimination, consistent with Title VI and the Americans with Disabilities Act.

definitions.definition: The individual a resident names to be notified and to act on the resident's behalf for the purposes allowed by the resident, such as receiving notices or having access to the resident.

The written, signed statement that the resident and designated person received, were told about, and had the chance to ask questions about the resident's rights and the right to complain without retaliation.

Any adverse action taken or threatened because a resident or another person raised a concern, made a complaint or used a right. Examples: reduced services, a changed room, threats of discharge, or less friendly treatment.
Any act that limits, withholds or conditions a resident's right, including using a right as a reward or a sanction.
The Department of Human Services poster of resident rights that the residence must display.

procedures: Before or at admission, the Administrator or designated admissions staff person gives the resident and the designated person a written copy of the Resident Rights statement. The statement includes the right to complain without retaliation and the complaint procedure in POL-07.

The staff person reviews the rights aloud, answers questions and uses the language or mode the person understands. This may mean an interpreter, a translated copy, large print, reading aloud or another accommodation under RR-03. The accommodation used is noted on the acknowledgment.

The resident and the designated person sign and date the Resident Rights Acknowledgment. The resident receives a copy. The original is filed in the resident record under POL-17 on the day of admission.
If a resident cannot sign or declines to sign, the staff person documents the reason and the witness. The Administrator then re-offers the rights review within 7 days and records the outcome.

The Administrator posts the current DHS rights poster in a conspicuous common area, [POSTER LOCATION]. The Administrator or designee checks monthly that the poster is displayed, legible and current, and initials the Forms Library check in FRM-04.
The Administrator posts the complaint hotline and agency numbers in large print next to the poster, as required by POL-07.

Before any new house rule takes effect, the Administrator gives each resident and designated person 30 days' written notice. Staff collect a signed receipt for each notice and file it in the resident record.

Staff may not withhold or condition phone use, mail, visitors, privacy, outings, records access or any other right as a reward, punishment or condition of care. A staff member who is asked to do so must refuse and report the request to the Administrator.

The Administrator reviews the contract, house rules and all admission paperwork (FRM-01) so that nothing asks a resident to waive a right. Any such language is void, is not enforced and is removed at the next revision.

Staff provide a private telephone and deliver mail unopened. Visitors are welcome at any time. The only limits on visitors are those the resident chooses or those needed to protect the safety of other residents.
Staff may not steer residents toward or away from any physician. Each resident chooses his or her own physician, and staff help with scheduling and transportation as described in POL-15.
When a resident needs to relocate, the Administrator provides relocation assistance under POL-16.

Whoever is at the front desk gives immediate access to DHS agents, the area agency on aging, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and the P&A system, with no appointment and no advance notice. That staff person escorts the visitor, makes residents and records available, and tells the Administrator at once. The visit is recorded in the Regulatory/Agency Visit Log.

If a resident asks for a designated person to have access, staff admit that person to the resident and the resident's records as the resident directs. Community and legal-services groups are admitted during posted visiting hours.
Every employee, volunteer and contractor learns resident rights at orientation and again each year (TRN-01, PLAN-01). Attendance is recorded in the training record.

Any staff member who sees or hears about a possible rights violation reports it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator records it as a complaint under POL-07. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is handled under SAF-01.
At least annually, the Administrator reviews rights acknowledgments, complaint log trends and poster checks with the Quality Management Plan (POL-03) and corrects any gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy. Ensures rights notification at admission, poster posting, 30-day notice of new rules, immediate access for authorized agencies, no retaliation, and annual review.
Deliver the rights statement, explain it in an understandable language or mode, obtain signatures and file the acknowledgment.

responsibilities.role: Direct care and all other staff
responsibilities.duty: Honor resident rights every day, never use rights as rewards or sanctions, and report concerns to the Administrator the same day.

responsibilities.role: Front desk or person in charge
responsibilities.duty: Give immediate access to DHS, the area agency on aging, the ombudsman and the P&A system, and log the visit.
May use, ask about and complain about rights at any time without retaliation.

documentation: Signed Resident Rights Acknowledgment in each resident record
Copy of the rights statement given to the resident
Documentation of language or mode accommodations
Monthly poster check entries in the Forms Library (FRM-04)
Signed receipts for 30-day written notice of new rules
Regulatory/Agency Visit Log
Staff rights training attendance records
Complaint log entries for rights concerns (POL-07)

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Voice-Controlled Electronic Devices and Real-Time Location Tracking Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all residents, staff and visitors
policies.purpose: To state plainly whether [AGENCY NAME] uses voice-controlled electronic devices or real-time location tracking systems, to protect residents' right to privacy, and to describe what must happen before either type of technology is introduced.
policies.policy:
This policy meets official checklist item 8(f), Use of Voice Controlled Electronic Devices (55 Pa. Code §2600.42(s); ALR counterpart §2800.42(s)), and item 8(g), Disclosure of their use and operational description of any real-time tracking location systems (55 Pa. Code §2600.42(s); ALR counterpart §2800.42(s)).

Item 8(f). [AGENCY NAME] does not install, own or operate voice-controlled electronic devices (such as smart speakers or voice assistants) in resident bedrooms, bathrooms or other private spaces. The residence does not use any device that listens to or records residents.

Item 8(g). [AGENCY NAME] does not use any real-time location tracking system on residents. It does not track residents' location through wearable devices, badges, phone applications or similar technology. Door alarms or other protective measures that may be used in a secured unit are described only in SCU-01 and SAF-03, and they do not give staff a continuous location record of a resident.

A resident may keep and use a personal voice-controlled device of his or her own. That is the resident's choice and is protected by the right to privacy in §2800.42. Staff will not use, operate or monitor a resident's personal device except at the resident's request.

If [AGENCY NAME] ever decides to use either technology, the Administrator will first revise this policy. The revision will state what the technology is and how it operates. It will also state where it is located, who can access any data, how long data is kept, and how privacy and consent are protected. It will give residents and designated persons 30 days' written notice (§2800.42), obtain each affected resident's written consent, and submit the revised policy to DHS before use begins. No resident will be required to accept either technology as a condition of admission or continued stay.

definitions.definition: Any device that listens for and responds to spoken commands, such as a smart speaker, voice assistant or voice-activated tablet or television, including devices that may record or transmit audio.
Any technology that determines and reports where a person is at a given moment or continuously, for example by wearable transmitters, badges, GPS devices or phone applications.
A device owned by a resident or designated person and used at the resident's choice, not provided or operated by the residence.
A resident's signed agreement made after being told in an understandable way what a technology does, what information it collects, who sees it, and that the resident may refuse.

procedures: The Administrator confirms that no voice-controlled device owned by [AGENCY NAME] is installed in any resident room, bathroom or common space, and that no real-time location tracking system is in use. The Administrator confirms this at policy adoption and at each annual policy review.
Admissions staff give each resident and designated person a copy of this policy with the admission disclosures (FRM-01) and note the review on the admission checklist.

When a resident brings a personal voice-controlled device, staff tell the resident it is allowed. Staff also remind the resident that other residents have privacy rights and that the device must not record roommates or visitors without their agreement.

In a shared room, staff ask the roommate whether he or she agrees to the device. If there is disagreement, the Administrator works out a solution that respects both residents' privacy, such as limiting the device's use to times or settings agreed by both.
Staff do not operate, set up, monitor or review a resident's personal device unless the resident asks. Staff never use such a device to listen to, record or locate a resident.

Staff do not use badge-based, wearable or phone-based tracking to follow a resident's movements. The only safety measures used are those documented in SCU-01 and SAF-03, and they are explained to the resident and designated person at admission.

Before any voice-controlled device or tracking technology is considered, the Administrator writes a proposal describing what it is, how it operates, where it would be used, what data it would collect, who could see the data and how long it would be kept.
The Administrator submits the proposal to the Quality Management review (POL-03) and checks it against the privacy rules in POL-02 and the residents' rights in POL-05.

If the proposal goes forward, the Administrator revises this policy, gives each resident and designated person 30 days' written notice with a plain-language description, and files a signed receipt in each resident record.

The Administrator obtains the signed informed written consent of each affected resident (or the resident's legally authorized representative) before use. Any resident who declines is not subject to the technology, and the refusal is recorded without penalty.
The Administrator submits the revised policy to the Bureau of Human Services Licensing before the technology is put into use and files the submission confirmation in the policy binder.

Staff who see an unauthorized recording or tracking device report it to the Administrator at once. The Administrator removes or stops its use and records the matter as a complaint (POL-07). If it may involve exploitation or abuse, the Administrator follows SAF-01.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and whenever technology in the residence changes, and records the review date on the policy.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy. Verifies no tracking or voice devices are used, approves or rejects any proposal, and ensures notice, consent and DHS submission occur before any future use.
Provide this policy at admission and answer questions about personal devices.
Respect residents' privacy, do not use or monitor devices to track or listen to residents, and report unauthorized devices to the Administrator.
May use personal devices at their own choice and may refuse any proposed technology.

documentation: This policy, with the date of each annual review
Admission checklist entry showing the policy was provided
Administrator's annual written confirmation that no voice-controlled devices or tracking systems are in use
For any future proposal: written description, 30-day notices and receipts, signed consents, DHS submission confirmation, and Quality Management review notes
Complaint log entries related to devices or recording (POL-07)

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Complaint Procedures and Complaint Log
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all residents, designated persons, families, staff and visitors
policies.purpose: To give residents and others a clear, safe way to raise concerns and to ensure each complaint is logged, answered and resolved on time without retaliation.
policies.policy:
This policy meets official checklist item 8(h), Complaint Procedures (55 Pa. Code §2600.44(a); ALR counterpart §2800.44).

Before admission, [AGENCY NAME] informs each resident and designated person that they may complain to [AGENCY NAME], to the Department of Human Services, to the long-term care ombudsman or protective services unit, to the Disability Rights Network, or to the police (§2800.44). We also tell them at admission that they may complain without retaliation (§2800.41). The residence keeps a Complaint Log. For each complaint, we give the complainant a status report within 2 business days and a written decision within 7 days. The complaint hotline number (1-877-401-8835) and agency numbers are posted in large print in the residence. No resident, family member, designated person or staff member will be punished, threatened, treated differently or discharged for making a complaint.

definitions.definition: Any concern, dissatisfaction or allegation about the residence, its staff, services or other residents, raised orally or in writing by a resident, designated person, family member, staff member or other person.
The running record of every complaint received, with the date, the complainant, the nature of the complaint, the dates of the status report and written decision, the resolution and any follow-up.
Communication to the complainant, within 2 business days of receiving the complaint, telling who is looking into it and what is being done.
A written response to the complainant, given within 7 days, stating the findings, the outcome and any action taken.
Any adverse action taken or threatened because someone made or supported a complaint.

procedures: Before admission, admissions staff give the resident and designated person the written complaint procedure. It lists the right to complain to the residence, DHS, the long-term care ombudsman or protective services unit, the Disability Rights Network and the police, with phone numbers: DHS Bureau of Human Services Licensing 717-783-3670; complaint hotline 1-877-401-8835; ombudsman [LTC OMBUDSMAN PHONE]; protective services [PROTECTIVE SERVICES PHONE]; Disability Rights Network [DISABILITY RIGHTS NETWORK PHONE]; police [LOCAL POLICE NON-EMERGENCY PHONE].
At admission, staff explain the right to complain without retaliation using the language or mode the person understands. The signed rights acknowledgment (POL-05) confirms that this was done.

The Administrator posts the complaint hotline number (1-877-401-8835) and the agency numbers in large print in [POSTING LOCATION], next to the rights poster, and checks monthly that the posting is legible and current.

Any staff member who receives a complaint, orally or in writing, records the date, the complainant, and the substance of the complaint and gives it to the Administrator by the end of that shift. Staff may help a resident write a complaint when asked.
A resident may submit a complaint anonymously, orally, in writing or through a designated person. Staff may not discourage a complaint or ask the person to withdraw it.

The Administrator enters the complaint in the Complaint Log within one business day of receipt. The entry includes the date received, the complainant, the nature of the complaint, and the staff involved.
The Administrator gives the complainant a status report within 2 business days of receiving the complaint, and records the date and manner of the report in the log.

The Administrator investigates promptly. This includes interviewing the complainant and relevant staff or residents, reviewing records, and observing the situation. No one involved in the matter may carry out the investigation alone.

The Administrator gives the complainant a written decision within 7 days of receiving the complaint. It states what was found, what action was taken or planned, and the complainant's right to take the complaint to any outside agency listed in this procedure. The date given is recorded in the log.

If the investigation is not complete within 7 days, the Administrator gives the written decision describing the findings to date and the planned next steps, and follows up in writing when the matter closes. Both dates are recorded.

If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator follows SAF-01 immediately. If it describes a reportable incident or condition, the Administrator follows POL-01. The complaint is still logged under this policy.

The Administrator protects the complainant from retaliation. Staff are reminded that retaliation is prohibited and may lead to discipline up to termination. The Administrator checks in with the complainant after resolution to confirm no retaliation has occurred and notes the check in the log.
The Administrator reviews the Complaint Log monthly for patterns and presents trends to the Quality Management review (POL-03), including corrective actions taken.
Complaint Log entries are kept in accordance with POL-17 and are made available to DHS and other authorized agencies on request (POL-05).
All staff are trained on this procedure at orientation and annually (TRN-01, PLAN-01).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the complaint process. Logs complaints, gives the 2-business-day status report and 7-day written decision, protects against retaliation, and reviews trends.
Give the complaint procedure before admission and explain the right to complain without retaliation at admission.
Accept every complaint without discouraging it, record it and hand it to the Administrator by the end of the shift, and never retaliate.
May complain at any time to the residence or directly to the outside agencies listed, without fear of retaliation.

documentation: Complaint Log, with dates of receipt, status report and written decision for every complaint
Copies of written decisions sent to complainants
Investigation notes and any corrective action
Signed rights acknowledgment confirming complaint procedure notice (POL-05)
Monthly posting check records for the hotline and agency numbers
Monthly Complaint Log review notes and Quality Management minutes (POL-03)
Staff training attendance records

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Swimming Pool Policy (if applicable)
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); applies only if the residence has a swimming pool
policies.purpose: To state whether [AGENCY NAME] has a swimming pool and to ensure that no pool is made available to residents until a written pool policy that meets DHS requirements has been adopted and submitted.
policies.policy:
This policy addresses official checklist item 8(i), Swimming Pools (if applicable) (55 Pa. Code §2600.106; ALR counterpart §2800.106). That item applies only if the residence has a swimming pool.

[AGENCY NAME] does not have a swimming pool at [ADDRESS], and none is available to residents. This statement is submitted in place of pool rules because the item is not applicable.

If [AGENCY NAME] later acquires, builds or gains access to a pool for resident use, the pool will remain closed to residents until the Administrator has read the full text of the pool regulation and written a pool policy that meets every requirement in it. The Administrator will give residents 30 days' written notice of the new rule and will submit the policy to the Bureau of Human Services Licensing. No pool specifics are stated in this version of the manual; they will be added only after the regulation has been read and applied.

definitions.definition: Any pool, spa or similar body of water on or controlled by the residence that is intended for resident use.
A statement that the residence does not have the facility or service the checklist item addresses.

procedures: The Administrator confirms at policy adoption that no swimming pool exists on the residence property and that no pool is under the residence's control. The confirmation is signed and dated and filed in the policy binder.
The submission to DHS states that the residence has no swimming pool and that item 8(i) is not applicable.
Admissions staff tell residents and visitors who ask that the residence has no pool.

Staff do not take residents to any outside pool as a residence-sponsored activity unless the Administrator has first approved it and Activities (DL-02) has documented supervision and safety arrangements.

Before acquiring, building, leasing or opening any pool for resident use, the Administrator notifies the Governing Body or owner [OWNER/GOVERNING BODY NAME] and puts the plan on the Quality Management agenda (POL-03).
The Administrator reads the full pool regulation (§2600.106 for a PCH or §2800.106 for an ALR) and the floor plan and fire-safety approval requirements (PLT-01).
The Administrator drafts a written pool policy that addresses every requirement in the regulation and any recommendations from the Bureau of Human Services Licensing.
The Administrator gives residents and designated persons 30 days' written notice of the new pool rules (POL-05) and gets signed receipts.
The Administrator submits the written pool policy to the Bureau of Human Services Licensing before any resident uses the pool, and keeps the submission confirmation.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and records that the residence still has no pool, or that a pool policy is in effect.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms and documents that there is no pool, and ensures no pool is opened without a compliant policy and DHS submission.
Notifies the Administrator before acquiring or building a pool and approves the pool policy.
Do not schedule pool activities unless the Administrator has approved them and the pool policy is in effect.

documentation: Signed Administrator confirmation that the residence has no swimming pool
DHS submission stating item 8(i) is not applicable
Annual policy review record
If a pool is later added: written pool policy, 30-day resident notices and receipts, DHS submission confirmation, and Quality Management minutes

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Emergency Preparedness Plan
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all residents, staff and visitors
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can protect residents and keep essential services running during fires, severe weather, utility outages, evacuations and other emergencies.
policies.policy:
This policy meets official checklist item 8(j), Emergency Preparedness Plan, including the 3-day drinking water requirement (55 Pa. Code §2600.107 and §2600.107(c); ALR counterpart §2800.107).

The Administrator holds a copy of the municipal emergency plan for [MUNICIPALITY]. [AGENCY NAME] maintains written emergency procedures that cover designated contacts, medical information for each resident, agency telephone numbers, transportation for relocation, staff duties during an emergency, and utility outages (§2800.107). We keep a 3-day supply of food and drinking water for all residents and staff.

Water supply under item 8(j). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a 3-day supply of drinking water at the residence, stored at [WATER STORAGE LOCATION]. If a 3-day supply will not be kept on site, we will submit a contract with a local bottled-water supplier that states the amount of water to be delivered immediately on request, 24 hours per day, with a guarantee of priority delivery even in a regional emergency. The Administrator chooses one of these two options before licensure, and the option chosen is documented in the plan.

The Administrator reviews the procedures at least annually and submits them to the local Emergency Management Agency (EMA). A utility termination is a reportable incident and is handled under POL-01.

definitions.definition: Any event that threatens residents' health or safety or disrupts essential services, including fire, flood, severe weather, loss of power, heat, water or telephone, a hazardous release, a missing resident, or an event requiring evacuation or relocation.
The person, named in the plan and in each resident record, who is called when an emergency affects a resident.
The county or municipal Emergency Management Agency, [LOCAL EMA NAME], that receives the residence's annual emergency procedures.
Food and drinking water sufficient for every resident and staff person on duty for 3 days, including any foods needed for therapeutic diets (DL-01).
Moving residents out of the residence temporarily or permanently because of an emergency.

procedures: The Administrator obtains the current emergency plan from [MUNICIPALITY] and keeps it in the Emergency Binder at [BINDER LOCATION]. The Administrator updates it whenever the municipality revises it.

The Administrator writes and maintains the residence's emergency procedures, covering designated contacts, resident medical information, agency numbers, relocation transportation, staff duties and utility outages.

Each resident's designated contact and emergency phone numbers are kept current in the resident record and in the Emergency Binder. Staff update them at admission, at each support plan review, and whenever a change is reported.

A current medical information sheet for each resident (diagnoses, medications, allergies, physician, advance directive status, mobility and communication needs) is printed monthly and kept in the Emergency Binder. It travels with the resident during any relocation.

The Emergency Binder contains agency and utility phone numbers: BHSL 717-783-3670; local EMA [LOCAL EMA PHONE]; fire, police and EMS [PHONE]; electric [UTILITY PHONE]; gas [UTILITY PHONE]; water [UTILITY PHONE]; the long-term care ombudsman [LTC OMBUDSMAN PHONE]; and the resident's physicians.
The Administrator arranges relocation transportation (written agreement with [TRANSPORT PROVIDER]), identifies a receiving location [RELOCATION SITE], and records the arrangements in the plan.

The plan assigns specific duties to each shift and position: who calls 911, who accounts for residents, who secures medications and records, who calls designated contacts, and who communicates with the Administrator and agencies. Duties are in STF-01.

For power, heat, water, telephone or other utility outages, the plan states the steps staff take, such as notifying the utility, using emergency lighting and portable heat, moving residents as needed, and contacting the Administrator. A termination of utilities is reported as required by POL-01.

The Administrator keeps a 3-day supply of non-perishable food and drinking water for every resident and staff person, and stores it at [FOOD AND WATER STORAGE LOCATION]. Therapeutic diet needs are included (DL-01). The Dietary lead checks the supply monthly, rotates stock, and records the check.

If drinking water will not be stored on site, the Administrator signs a contract with [BOTTLED WATER SUPPLIER] stating the volume delivered immediately on request, 24 hours per day, with a guarantee of priority delivery during a regional emergency. A copy of the contract is attached to the plan and submitted with the licensing materials.
The Administrator trains all staff on the plan at orientation and annually, and records attendance (TRN-01, PLAN-01). Fire drills and evacuation practice follow SAF-04.
During an emergency, the person in charge follows the plan, calls 911 when needed, accounts for every resident, notifies the Administrator and designated contacts, and documents actions and times.
After any emergency or drill, the Administrator holds a debrief within 7 days, records what worked and what did not, and updates the plan.
At least once a year, the Administrator reviews the written procedures and submits them to the local EMA. The submission date and any EMA response are filed in the Emergency Binder.
Any utility termination, evacuation or relocation is reported as a reportable incident under POL-01, and the emergency medical plan (POL-12) is used for medical needs.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the plan; keeps the municipal plan; reviews and submits procedures to the local EMA each year; arranges transportation and water; reports utility terminations.

responsibilities.role: Person in charge on each shift
responsibilities.duty: Directs staff, calls 911, accounts for residents and uses the Emergency Binder.
Carry out assigned emergency duties and assist residents.
Maintains and rotates the 3-day food and water supply and records monthly checks.
Tests emergency lighting and supplies, and handles utility outages.

documentation: Municipal emergency plan on file
Written emergency procedures and annual review record
Annual submission to the local EMA with date and confirmation
Emergency Binder: contacts, resident medical information sheets, agency numbers
Relocation transportation agreement and relocation site arrangement
Monthly food and water supply check log, or bottled-water supplier contract with 24-hour priority delivery
Staff emergency training records and drill/debrief reports
Incident reports for any utility termination or relocation (POL-01)

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Firearms and Weapons Policy
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all residents, staff, volunteers, contractors and visitors on the premises
policies.purpose: To keep residents, staff and visitors safe by controlling firearms, ammunition and other weapons at the residence.
policies.policy:
This policy meets official checklist item 8(k), Firearms and Weapons Policy (if applicable) (55 Pa. Code §2600.108(5); ALR counterpart §2800.108).

[AGENCY NAME] does not permit firearms, ammunition or other weapons in resident rooms, common areas or any other part of the residence, except as stated here. Residents, staff, volunteers, contractors and visitors may not bring or keep weapons on the premises. This does not apply to on-duty law enforcement officers.

If a weapon or ammunition is found or is brought to the residence, it is surrendered to the Administrator or designee. It is stored only in a locked cabinet at [LOCKED CABINET LOCATION], with ammunition stored separately from any firearm, and the key held only by the Administrator or designee (§2800.108(d)). The weapon is held there until it is removed from the premises by the owner or turned over to law enforcement. Weapons are never stored in resident rooms or the secured unit.

definitions.definition: Any handgun, rifle, shotgun or other device designed to expel a projectile by explosive force, including antique and non-working firearms.
Any firearm, ammunition, knife with a blade intended as a weapon, club, stun device, explosive or other item capable of causing serious harm and not needed for ordinary daily living.
The staff person named in writing by the Administrator to hold the weapons cabinet key in the Administrator's absence.
A secure cabinet that only the Administrator or designee can open, used for weapon storage and not for other items.

procedures: At pre-admission screening (AR-01), staff ask the prospective resident and designated person whether the resident owns or intends to bring any firearm, ammunition or other weapon, and explain that weapons are not permitted in the residence.
The Resident-Residence Contract and admission disclosures (FRM-01) state this policy. The resident or designated person signs that they received and understood it.
The Administrator names a designee in writing and records the designee's name in the staff list (ORG-01). Only the Administrator and the designee hold keys to the weapons cabinet.
Staff, volunteers and contractors are told of this policy at orientation (TRN-01) and agree in writing not to bring weapons onto the premises.
Staff who see or learn of a weapon on the premises tell the Administrator or person in charge at once. They do not handle a firearm themselves unless necessary to prevent immediate harm.
If a person is in immediate danger, staff move residents to safety and call 911.

The Administrator or designee takes custody of the weapon, unloads it only if trained and it is safe to do so, and places firearms and ammunition in separate compartments of the locked cabinet. Ammunition is always kept separate from the firearm.
The Administrator or designee records the date, time, who surrendered the item, a description of the item and serial number, and who received it in the Weapons Storage Log.

The Administrator notifies the owner and arranges for removal from the premises. If the owner is a resident, the designated person is notified. If the owner cannot be reached or the item is illegal, the Administrator contacts local police at [LOCAL POLICE PHONE] to take custody.
When the item is released, the Administrator records the date, recipient and signature in the log.
The Administrator checks the cabinet and log monthly to verify the key is controlled and contents match the log, and records the check.
If a weapon is used or threatened against anyone, the Administrator follows POL-01 for reportable incidents and SAF-01 where abuse or exploitation may be involved.

Residents who have a lawful need for an item that could be a weapon in ordinary use, such as a kitchen knife in a supervised activity, are assessed individually. The decision is documented in the support plan (FRM-03).
The Administrator reviews this policy annually and gives 30 days' written notice of any change to residents (POL-05).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the policy; controls the cabinet key; takes custody of surrendered weapons; notifies owner and police; reviews the log monthly.
Holds the cabinet key in the Administrator's absence and follows custody and logging procedures.
Ask about weapons at pre-admission screening and provide this policy with the admission disclosures.
Do not bring weapons; report any weapon to the Administrator at once.
Do not bring weapons into the residence.

documentation: This policy, with annual review date
Signed admission disclosure of the weapons policy in each resident record
Staff orientation acknowledgment of the policy
Written designee appointment
Weapons Storage Log, including surrender and release entries
Monthly cabinet and key control checks
Incident reports for any weapon found, used or threatened (POL-01)

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Inoperable Fire Alarm and Smoke Detector Policy
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all staff, maintenance personnel, administrator and designee
policies.purpose: To make sure that a defective smoke detector or fire alarm component at [AGENCY NAME] is found quickly, repaired or replaced within 48 hours, and covered by interim safeguards so residents stay protected until the repair is finished.
policies.policy: This policy meets item 8(l), Inoperable Fire Alarm/Smoke Detector Policy (§ 2600.130(h)), and is the written procedure required by 55 Pa. Code §2800.130(g). [AGENCY NAME] will have a working smoke detector in each living unit, tested monthly with a written record. Any defective smoke detector will be repaired or replaced within 48 hours of discovery. If the residence has 9 or more residents, it will keep an interconnected fire alarm. If 5 or more residents have mobility needs, it will keep a monitored connection. When any detector, alarm panel, interconnection or monitoring connection is inoperable, the interim safeguards in this policy start at once. The most important is a documented fire watch, which stays in place until the system is tested and restored. Extinguishers are maintained as required by 55 Pa. Code §§2800.130–2800.131: 2-A extinguishers on each floor and for every 3,000 square feet, a 2A-10BC extinguisher in the kitchen, and annual inspection.

definitions.definition: Any smoke detector, alarm panel, horn/strobe, interconnection or monitoring connection that fails a test, shows a trouble or fault signal, has no power or battery, has been removed or disabled, or is otherwise unable to sound or transmit an alarm.

A temporary protective measure used while equipment is out of service. Examples are a fire watch, a battery-powered temporary detector, additional staff rounds, or relocation of a resident with the resident's consent.

A documented, scheduled walk-through of all affected areas by a trained staff person whose only task is to look for signs of fire and, if one is found, to sound the alarm, call 911 and begin evacuation.
A connection that sends fire alarm signals to a monitoring company or fire department outside the residence.

procedures: The administrator or designee ensures that every living unit has a working smoke detector, and that detectors and alarm devices are installed as shown on the fire-safety-approved floor plan (see PLT-01).

Maintenance staff [MAINTENANCE PERSON/TITLE] tests every smoke detector monthly. The Smoke Detector Test Log (kept in the forms library, FRM-04) records the date, unit or location, tester's name, result (pass/fail), and any corrective action.
The tester reports any failed or missing detector to the administrator or designee immediately, and the administrator or designee takes the interim safeguards in step 5 on the same shift.

Any staff member or resident who notices a chirping, silent, blocked, damaged or removed detector, or an alarm panel trouble signal, tells the person in charge immediately. Staff never silence, cover or disable a detector without replacing it with a working one.

Interim safeguards: (a) install a working temporary battery-powered detector in the unit if one is available; (b) start a fire watch of the affected unit or area; (c) tell all staff on duty and later shifts about the problem at the shift report; (d) if the unit cannot be protected, offer the resident a temporary move to a unit with a working detector and document the resident's choice.
The administrator or designee records on the Inoperable Smoke Detector/Fire Alarm Record the date and time of discovery, location, who found it, cause if known, and the interim safeguards started.
The detector is repaired or replaced within 48 hours of discovery. The repair is recorded with the date, time, who made it, and the result of the test performed afterward.

If the repair cannot be completed within 48 hours, the administrator or designee continues the fire watch without interruption, documents why the repair is delayed and the expected completion date, and orders the part or contractor the same day.

If the alarm panel, interconnection or monitored connection is out of service, the person in charge starts a fire watch at once, notifies the administrator, and calls the alarm contractor [ALARM VENDOR, PHONE] the same day. If a monitored connection is out, the person in charge also tells the monitoring company and the local fire department non-emergency line that monitoring is interrupted.

Fire watch requirements: a trained staff person is assigned who has no other duties during the watch. The person walks all resident areas, exits and the kitchen at least every 30 minutes, carries a working telephone, and signs the Fire Watch Log with the time of each round. The watch continues around the clock until the system is tested and working.

During any outage the person in charge confirms that exits are clear, extinguishers are in place and charged, and staff on duty know the evacuation routes and each resident's evacuation needs (see SAF-04).

After repair, maintenance staff tests the repaired device. For a panel or interconnection repair, all devices are tested and the result is recorded. The administrator or designee signs the record to end the fire watch.

The administrator reviews each outage to find a cause (for example, dead batteries, tampering or aged equipment) and corrects it, such as by replacing aging detectors or adjusting the battery-change schedule.
The administrator evaluates whether the event, or any fire-related harm to a resident, is a reportable incident under POL-01, and reports it as required.
A licensed contractor inspects the fire alarm system and extinguishers annually. The inspection report and tags are kept on site and made available to the Department at inspection (see GOV-01).
Fire alarm and smoke detector outage records are reviewed at the quality management meeting each quarter (see POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures detectors and alarms are installed and maintained, assigns the fire watch, approves repairs and the end of the watch, evaluates reportability, and keeps records.
Starts interim safeguards immediately when the administrator is absent, documents the outage and notifies the administrator.
Tests detectors monthly, repairs or replaces defective devices within 48 hours, and logs the work.
Report any inoperable device immediately, perform fire watch rounds when assigned, and keep exits clear.
Performs repairs and the annual inspection and provides written reports.

documentation: Smoke Detector Test Log (monthly)
Inoperable Smoke Detector/Fire Alarm Record
Fire Watch Log
Annual fire alarm and extinguisher inspection reports
Contractor service invoices and repair records
Quality management minutes noting outages

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Emergency Medical Plan
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all staff, administrator and designee
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident gets prompt emergency medical care, that the information needed for treatment goes with the resident, and that staff know whom to call, where to send residents and who is responsible.
policies.policy: This policy meets item 8(m), Emergency Medical Plan (§ 2600.143(a)), and the written emergency medical plan required by 55 Pa. Code §2800.143(a). [AGENCY NAME] will help residents obtain medical care (55 Pa. Code §2800.142). The written plan names the hospital, the means of transportation and the staffing that will respond to a medical emergency. Emergency data, including any advance directive and DNR order, goes with the resident to the hospital. Staff give CPR unless the resident has a valid DNR order. Refusals of care, and efforts to obtain consent, are documented.

definitions.definition: A sudden illness, injury or change in condition that threatens life, limb or health and needs immediate professional medical attention.

The resident's face sheet, current medication list, diagnoses, allergies, physician and prescriber contacts, designated person and emergency contacts, insurance information, and copies of any advance directive and DNR order.
A do-not-resuscitate order signed by the resident's physician, PA or CRNP and kept in the resident's record.
The person the resident has named to be notified of changes or emergencies.

procedures: The administrator keeps a written Emergency Medical Plan that names the primary hospital [HOSPITAL NAME, ADDRESS, PHONE], an alternate hospital [ALTERNATE HOSPITAL], the ambulance or transport service [AMBULANCE SERVICE, PHONE], and the staff person responsible on each shift. The plan is reviewed annually and whenever a name or number changes.

The plan and emergency numbers (911, hospital, poison control, administrator on call [PHONE], BHSL complaint line number as posted) are posted at each staff station and are available to every staff person on every shift.

At admission, the administrator or designee prepares each resident's emergency data packet from the medical evaluation, assessment and contract. The packet includes the advance directive and DNR order if the resident has them (see RR-02). It is updated at least whenever medications, diagnoses or contacts change, and is stored in a location known to all shifts.
Each shift has at least one staff person with current first aid and CPR training on duty, as set out in STF-02. The shift's emergency staff person is named on the daily assignment sheet.
When a resident has a medical emergency, the first staff person on the scene stays with the resident, calls for help from another staff person and, for any life-threatening condition, calls 911.

Staff give first aid. If the resident has no pulse or is not breathing, staff begin CPR and continue until emergency responders arrive, unless a valid DNR order is in the resident's record. If a DNR is in place, staff do not perform CPR, keep the resident comfortable, and show the DNR order to responders.
A second staff person retrieves the emergency data packet and gives it to the transport crew, so that it goes with the resident, with any advance directive and DNR order included.

If the resident is transported, a staff person tells the hospital the resident's name, medical problems, allergies and medications, and gives the name and number of the designated person and the administrator.
Staff notify the designated person, the resident's physician or prescriber, and the administrator or designee as soon as the emergency is under control, and no later than the same shift.

When the resident cannot make decisions and no designated person can be reached, staff continue to seek consent from the designated person, the resident's representative or the health care agent, and document every attempt (who was called, time, result). Staff never delay emergency treatment while attempting to obtain consent.

If a resident refuses emergency or other medical care, staff explain the risks, offer to call the physician or designated person, respect the resident's right to refuse when the resident has capacity, and document the refusal, what was explained, who was notified, and the resident's condition.
The person in charge records the event on an incident report the same shift. The administrator evaluates it under POL-01 and the resident's change of condition under HC-01.

When the resident returns from the hospital, the administrator or designee obtains discharge instructions and new orders, reconciles medications (see POL-14), and updates the assessment and support plan (see FRM-03).
Staff practice the plan through a drill or review at orientation and at least annually, and the results are recorded in staff training records (see PLAN-01).
The administrator reviews emergency events at each quality management meeting to find ways to improve response time and documentation (see POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Writes and updates the plan, ensures emergency data packets are current, and reviews each emergency.
Directs the response on the shift, makes sure notifications are completed, and completes the incident report.
Provide first aid and CPR (unless a DNR is in place), call 911, and give emergency data to responders.
Advises on emergency protocols and reviews outcomes (see HC-01).

documentation: Written Emergency Medical Plan
Emergency data packet for each resident
Advance directive/DNR copies
Incident report
Documentation of refusals and attempts to obtain consent
First aid/CPR training records
Drill or review records

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Smoking Policy, Pets and Visitors
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); residents, visitors, staff and the administrator
policies.purpose: To tell residents, families and staff whether smoking and pets are permitted at [AGENCY NAME], to set fire-safety and health rules when they are, and to protect each resident's right to have visitors at any time.
policies.policy: This policy meets item 8(n), Smoking Policy (if applicable) (§ 2600.144(b)-(c)). Under 55 Pa. Code §2800.144, [AGENCY NAME] states in its rules whether the residence is smoking or nonsmoking. The residence is: [NONSMOKING / SMOKING-PERMITTED — administrator to select one before opening]. If smoking is permitted, the written fire-safety rules in this policy apply: a designated smoking area, fireproof receptacles, extinguishers, no tobacco use during transportation, and no smoking outside the designated area. Under 55 Pa. Code §§2800.108–2800.109, this policy also states whether pets are allowed: [PETS ARE / ARE NOT ALLOWED]. Where pets are allowed, cats and dogs must have current rabies certificates, and any pet charges are stated in the resident contract. Under 55 Pa. Code §2800.42, residents may have visitors at any time, and [AGENCY NAME] gives 30 days' written notice of any new rule.

definitions.definition: The location named in this policy, approved by the administrator, where smoking is the only permitted place for tobacco use.
Smoking, vaping or other use of cigarettes, cigars, pipes or other tobacco or nicotine products.
A non-combustible container with a lid or other means of extinguishing smoking materials.
A cat, dog or other animal kept at the residence for companionship that is not a service animal.

procedures: Before opening, the administrator selects the smoking status (nonsmoking or smoking-permitted) and the pet status (allowed or not allowed), records the decision in the residence rules, and makes sure the resident contract and admission disclosure match (see FRM-01).

At the time of admission, the administrator or designee gives each resident and the resident's designated person a copy of the rules, reviews the smoking, pet and visitor rules, and records that this was done.
If any rule changes, the administrator gives each resident 30 days' written notice before the change takes effect and keeps a copy of the notice.
