NONSMOKING residence: no tobacco use is allowed inside the residence or in any residence vehicle. The administrator posts clear signs at each entrance. Staff tell visitors and residents where outdoor tobacco use is allowed, if anywhere.

SMOKING-PERMITTED residence: tobacco use is allowed only in the designated smoking area [DESIGNATED AREA DESCRIPTION]. Smoking in a resident's room or any other part of the residence is not permitted.

The designated smoking area has fireproof receptacles, at least one fire extinguisher, a sign and adequate ventilation, and staff empty receptacles into a metal container with a lid at least daily. Staff check the area at each shift.
Tobacco use is not permitted during transportation provided by the residence, including by the driver and by residents.

Staff assess whether a resident can smoke safely using the assessment (see FRM-03). Residents who cannot smoke safely independently are offered supervision, a staff-held lighter or other arrangements recorded in the support plan.

Staff tell residents who smoke elsewhere, and staff who find smoking materials in other areas, to stop and report to the administrator. The event is documented, and fire-safety risks are assessed under SAF-04.

Pets, if not allowed: no pets may live at the residence. Service animals and visits by animals brought by visitors are handled as the administrator permits, and the resident is told this at admission.

Pets, if allowed: before a pet is admitted, the resident gives the administrator current rabies certificates for each cat and dog, signed by a veterinarian. The administrator keeps a copy in the resident's record and tracks the expiration date.

Pet charges, such as a deposit or fee, are stated in the resident contract (see FRM-01). The resident is responsible for the pet's food, care, waste removal and damage, and staff do not provide pet care unless stated in the contract.

The administrator may require removal of a pet that threatens the safety or health of residents or staff, or whose rabies certificate expires and is not renewed, after talking with the resident and documenting the reason.

Residents may have visitors at any time. [AGENCY NAME] does not set visiting hours. A visitor may be asked to sign in so staff know who is in the building in an emergency, but signing in is not a condition of visiting.

A resident's right to private visits, phone and mail is protected. Staff respect a resident's request not to see a particular visitor. The administrator may restrict a visitor only when the visitor threatens the safety of residents or staff, or has an illness that endangers residents (see SAF-05), and documents the reason.
Ombudsman and advocacy representatives are allowed to visit residents at any time (see POL-05).

responsibilities.duty: Selects and publishes the smoking, pet and visitor rules, gives 30-day notice of changes, approves the smoking area and pet admissions, and keeps rabies certificates.
Enforce the rules, supervise smoking when assessed as needed, empty receptacles, and welcome visitors.
Follow the posted rules and use designated areas.
Maintain extinguishers and receptacles in the smoking area.

documentation: Written residence rules
Signed acknowledgment of rules at admission
30-day notices of rule changes
Pet rabies certificates and expiration tracking
Smoking-area daily check log (if smoking is permitted)
Smoking safety assessment and support plan notes
Restriction-of-visitor documentation, if any

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Medication Administration, Storage and Disposal Policy
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); administrator, nurse, medication-trained staff
policies.purpose: To make sure residents get their medications safely, on time and as prescribed; that only authorized staff administer them; that medications are stored, accounted for and destroyed properly; and that all medication events are documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets item 8(o), Medication Administration Policy (§ 2600.185(a)-(b), § 2600.188(d)), and item 10(h), The home's forms for: Medication Administration Record (§ 2600.187(a)). Under 55 Pa. Code §§2800.181–2800.191, [AGENCY NAME] assists residents with self-administration according to the assessment, and a physician, PA or CRNP must assess residents who self-administer. Staff may administer medication only if they are licensed to do so or have completed DHS-approved medication administration training (oral, topical, eye/nose/ear, insulin, epinephrine). Medications and syringes are kept locked in labeled original containers, and are not removed more than 2 hours before administration. Prescriber orders are written. A medication record is kept for each administration. Refusals are reported to the prescriber within 24 hours. Medication errors are reported immediately to the resident, the designated person and the prescriber. Adverse reactions prompt immediate physician consultation. Discontinued and expired medications are destroyed safely, and a departing resident's medications go with the resident. Each resident is educated on the right to question or refuse a medication.

definitions.definition: A resident taking his or her own medication, with only reminders or physical help such as opening a container, as allowed by the assessment.
Giving a medication to a resident by a licensed person or trained staff according to a prescriber's order.
The form on which each dose given, refused or missed is recorded at the time of administration.
A wrong drug, dose, time, route or resident, a missed dose, or administration without an order.
An unexpected or harmful reaction to a medication.

procedures: Before admission, the administrator or designee obtains the resident's medical evaluation and a current medication list (see FRM-02). The prescriber's written order is on file for every prescription and over-the-counter medication, and for every treatment.

At admission and when the condition changes, the assessment records whether the resident can self-administer, needs assistance with self-administration, or needs staff administration (see FRM-03). A physician, PA or CRNP assesses every resident who self-administers, and the finding is kept in the record.

Only staff who are licensed to administer medications, or who have completed the DHS-approved medication administration course with a performance test passed within the past 2 years, administer medications. Staff who give insulin must also have completed DHS-approved diabetes education within the past 12 months. The administrator verifies each person's certificate before assigning medication duties and keeps copies in the training records (see PLAN-01).
The administrator keeps a current list of staff authorized to administer, by route (oral, topical, eye/nose/ear, insulin injection, epinephrine). Staff only perform tasks on the list.

Before each pass, the authorized staff person washes hands, checks the MAR against the label (resident, drug, dose, route, time), and administers only what is ordered. Staff never use one resident's medication for another resident.
Staff do not remove (pour or set up) a medication from its container more than 2 hours before it is to be given. Medications stay in their labeled original containers until given.

Immediately after the resident takes the dose, staff initial the MAR with date and time. The MAR is completed for every administration. Each entry shows the resident's name, drug name, dose, route, frequency, time due, time given, staff initials and signature, and the prescriber. PRN doses also record the reason and result.

When a resident refuses a dose, staff do not force it, record the refusal on the MAR, and report the refusal to the prescriber within 24 hours. Staff also tell the administrator or designee and document the follow-up in the resident's record.

Each resident is told, and the instruction recorded, that the resident has the right to question or refuse any medication. Staff explain each new medication's purpose and common side effects in plain language.

Storage: all medications, including over-the-counter medications and syringes, are kept in locked storage in labeled original containers. Refrigerated medications are kept in a locked container or a locked refrigerator. External-use products are separated from internal ones. Keys are held only by authorized staff.

Receipt: when a medication is delivered, the staff person checks it against the order, signs the receipt record, and files the pharmacy documentation. Controlled substances are counted with a second staff person on receipt and at each shift change, and counts are recorded.

Missing medication: staff who discover a missing medication tell the administrator at once. The administrator searches, reviews the MAR and counts, records the findings, notifies the prescriber and, when theft is suspected, notifies the police and evaluates the event under POL-01.

Medication errors: the staff person who discovers an error ensures the resident is safe, then immediately reports it to the resident, the designated person and the prescriber. The staff person writes an incident report the same shift documenting the error and the follow-up, and the administrator reviews for cause and corrective action (see POL-03).

Adverse reactions: staff consult the physician at once. For serious symptoms such as trouble breathing or swelling, staff call 911 (see POL-12). The reaction is documented in the record and on the MAR.

Disposal: discontinued, expired or unused medications are removed from the cart and destroyed in a safe manner [DISPOSAL METHOD, E.G., PHARMACY TAKE-BACK OR DRUG DEACTIVATION SYSTEM] by two staff who sign a destruction record showing resident, drug, amount, date and method. Controlled substances are destroyed by the method required by law.

When a resident leaves the residence, the administrator or designee sends the resident's medications along with the resident, with a current list of medications, and records what was sent and who received it. When a resident dies, medications are handled under HC-02 and POL-17.
The administrator reviews MARs monthly for missing initials or unreported refusals, audits storage and counts, and presents medication findings at quality management meetings.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies staff authorization and training, audits MARs and storage, and ensures reporting of refusals and errors.
Reviews medication orders and assessments, advises on errors and reactions, and trains staff as needed.
Administer or assist with medications as authorized, complete MARs, report refusals, errors and reactions.
Provides written orders and responds to reports of refusals, errors and reactions.

documentation: Medication Administration Record (MAR) for each resident
Prescriber orders
Self-administration assessments
Medication training certificates and diabetes education records
Receipt records and controlled substance counts
Refusal and error documentation and incident reports
Destruction record
Record of medications sent with departing resident
Documentation of resident education on the right to refuse or question

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Description of Services Policy
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); administrator, staff, and prospective and current residents
policies.purpose: To state clearly which services [AGENCY NAME] offers, which services it does not offer but will help residents coordinate, and the admission and discharge criteria, so residents can choose the residence knowing what to expect.
policies.policy: This policy meets item 8(p), Description of Services Policy based upon all services offered and those not offered but the home will coordinate which may include Dementia/Memory Care, Brain Injury Care, Mental Health Services, Intellectual Disability/Autism Care, Hospice Care, Respite Care (§ 2600.223(a)-(b), § 2600.231(a)-(h)). Under 55 Pa. Code §§2800.220–2800.223, [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written description of services with admission and discharge criteria and written procedures. It provides the §2800.220(b) services (meals, laundry, activities, ADL/IADL help, medication help, housekeeping, transportation, 24-hour supervision and cognitive support) and offers the Independent and Enhanced core service packages. Only a licensed residence may use the term 'assisted living.' Hospice care and services licensed by the Department of Health may be provided in the residence (55 Pa. Code §2800.29). Dementia care in a special care unit is provided only if the unit is approved under 55 Pa. Code §§2800.231–2800.239.

definitions.definition: The written document stating each service offered, services coordinated with outside providers, the core packages, admission and discharge criteria, and the procedures for providing services.
The set of services included in the Independent or Enhanced package, with the cost stated in the contract.
A service not provided by [AGENCY NAME] staff that the residence helps the resident arrange with an outside licensed provider.
A secured unit or area for residents with Alzheimer's disease or dementia, approved by the Department before opening.

procedures: The administrator prepares the written Description of Services before opening and reviews it at least annually and whenever a service changes. It lists every service offered, every service coordinated but not offered, the core packages, and the admission and discharge criteria.

The Description of Services lists the services required by §2800.220(b): meals; laundry; activities; help with activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs); medication help; housekeeping; transportation; 24-hour supervision; and cognitive support. The description states how each is delivered, by whom and when.

The description defines the Independent core package and the Enhanced core package offered by [AGENCY NAME], states which services are included in each, and states the charges in the contract (see FRM-01 and RR-01).

Dementia/memory care: [AGENCY NAME] [DOES / DOES NOT] operate a special care unit. If it does, it applies to the Department 60 days before opening the unit; performs a cognitive screening within 72 hours before admission and reassesses quarterly; provides 8 hours of initial and 8 hours of annual staff training; offers weekly unit activities; obtains lock approvals; has wandering-prevention measures; and meets the 2-hour-per-day staffing rule for every resident (see SCU-01, SCU-02 and SCU-03). If it does not, residents with dementia whose needs exceed the residence's services are referred to an approved special care unit.

Brain injury care: [AGENCY NAME] [OFFERS / DOES NOT OFFER] services specific to brain injury. If not offered, staff help the resident and designated person to find a specialized provider or program and coordinate with it when the resident continues to live at the residence.

Mental health services: the residence does not provide clinical mental health treatment. Staff help residents arrange outpatient mental health services, transport them to appointments, and coordinate with the provider's recommendations as set out in the support plan.

Intellectual disability/autism care: [AGENCY NAME] [OFFERS / DOES NOT OFFER] specialized services. If not offered, staff help residents connect with county and state services, and the residence admits the resident only if it can meet the resident's needs under the admission criteria.

Hospice care: hospice care and services licensed by the Department of Health may be provided in the residence. The administrator coordinates with the hospice agency chosen by the resident, as set out in HC-02, and the hospice plan is added to the support plan.

Respite care: [AGENCY NAME] [OFFERS / DOES NOT OFFER] short-term respite stays. If offered, a respite resident meets the same pre-admission screening, medical evaluation, assessment and contract requirements as any resident (see AR-01 and FRM-01), and the stay's length and charges are in writing.

Admission criteria: the description states who may be admitted, based on the pre-admission screening, medical evaluation and assessment, and that residents with excludable conditions are not admitted or retained unless the Department grants an exception (see POL-16 and AR-01).

Discharge criteria: the description states the grounds on which a resident may be discharged, the 30-day written notice, and the aging-in-place accommodations the residence will try first (see POL-16).

Written procedures: the description cross-references the procedures for each service, such as medication (POL-14), nursing (HC-01), food service (DL-01), and activities, transportation and housekeeping (DL-02).
The administrator gives a copy of the Description of Services to each prospective resident before admission and to each resident at the time of any change, and records the date given.

Staff provide only the services listed. If a resident asks for a service not listed, the administrator decides whether it can be added, documents the decision and, if added, updates the support plan and, if there is a cost, the contract.
The administrator uses 'assisted living' only in connection with the licensed residence and checks marketing materials, signs and website for accurate service descriptions (see GOV-01).
The Description of Services is kept on file, available to the Department at inspection, and reviewed at quality management meetings (see POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Writes, updates and distributes the Description of Services, verifies marketing accuracy and approves changes.
Advises on which care needs the residence can meet and on coordination with hospice and other providers.
Deliver services as described and help residents coordinate outside services.
Review the description with prospective residents and document delivery.

documentation: Written Description of Services with admission and discharge criteria
Core service package schedules
Record of delivery of the description to each resident
SCU approval documents (if applicable)
Hospice coordination records
Referral and coordination notes for services not offered

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Retention Limits Policy
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); administrator, designee, nurse and residents
policies.purpose: To protect residents from improper or unsafe discharge or transfer, to set clear limits on conditions the residence may not keep, and to make sure residents get proper notice and help moving.
policies.policy: This policy meets item 8(q), Discharge/Transfer Policy (§ 2600.228(b)). Under 55 Pa. Code §2800.228, [AGENCY NAME] gives 30 days' written notice of transfer or discharge stating the reason, the date, the destination and the ombudsman contact. Discharge is allowed only on the grounds listed in the regulation, and only after the residence has attempted aging-in-place accommodation. If the residence closes, it gives the Department 60 days' notice. A discharge tracking chart is kept. Under 55 Pa. Code §2800.229, the residence does not admit or retain a resident with ventilator dependency, an unhealed Stage III or IV pressure ulcer, continuous IV fluids, a communicable-state infectious disease, a nasogastric tube, restraints, or a need for 24-hour skilled nursing, unless the Department grants an exception. Under 55 Pa. Code §2800.25, the resident contract is month-to-month, requiring 14 days' notice from the resident and 30 days' notice from the residence.

definitions.definition: The end of a resident's stay at the residence, whether the resident goes home, to another residence, to a nursing facility or elsewhere.
The move of a resident to another setting, such as a hospital or other residence.
A reasonable change in services, supports, schedule or environment that lets a resident stay at the residence as needs change.
A condition listed in §2800.229 that the residence may not admit or retain without a Department exception.
The Long-Term Care Ombudsman program, which advocates for residents and must be named in discharge notices.

procedures: The administrator reviews every prospective resident against the excludable conditions at pre-admission screening (see AR-01) and does not admit anyone with an excludable condition unless the Department has granted an exception in writing.

If an exception is requested, the administrator documents the resident's condition, the services that will meet the resident's needs, and the physician or prescriber statement, submits the request to the Department, and keeps the request and the Department's answer in the exception records. No excludable-condition resident is admitted until the exception is granted.
The nurse or designee reviews each resident's condition at each assessment (see FRM-03) and whenever the condition changes (see HC-01) to see whether an excludable condition has developed.

If an excludable condition or other change develops, the administrator meets with the resident, the designated person and the resident's physician to look at aging-in-place accommodations (more services, adjusted schedule, outside providers or hospice, see HC-02), and documents each option tried and its result.

If the needs cannot be met after those accommodations, or if another listed ground for discharge applies, the administrator confirms the ground in writing against the list in 55 Pa. Code §2800.228 and decides on discharge. Discharge on a ground not listed is not permitted.

The administrator gives the resident and the designated person written notice at least 30 days before the discharge date. The notice states the specific reason, the discharge date, the destination, and the ombudsman's contact information, and advises the resident of the right to ask for help with relocation.

The administrator reviews the notice with the resident in person in plain language or in the resident's language (see RR-03), gives the resident a copy and records the date and the person who received it.

The administrator helps the resident and the designated person find an appropriate placement, contacts potential providers, arranges transportation, shares the records with the resident's consent, and arranges follow-up with the resident's physician, so the resident is not left without a safe destination.

A resident may give 14 days' written notice to leave under the month-to-month contract (see FRM-01). The administrator acknowledges the notice in writing, plans the discharge date, refunds amounts as required by the contract and RR-01, and records the date of the notice.

On or before the discharge date, staff return the resident's money and personal property, give the resident the medications and current list (see POL-14), and send required records and instructions to the receiving provider.

If a resident must go to a hospital, staff follow POL-12 and HC-01. The administrator decides whether the resident may return, applying the retention limits in this policy and any bed-hold terms in the contract.

Emergency transfers needed to protect the health or safety of the resident or others begin with immediate action, such as calling 911. The administrator then gives written notice as soon as possible and documents the circumstances.

The administrator enters each discharge and transfer on the discharge tracking chart, showing resident, date, reason, ground relied upon, accommodations tried, destination and notice date, and reviews the chart at quality management meetings (see POL-03).

If [AGENCY NAME] plans to close, the administrator gives the Department 60 days' written notice, notifies each resident and designated person in writing, helps each resident relocate, and arranges the secure transfer of records and funds (see POL-17).
The administrator reports as required any discharge related to an incident covered by POL-01, and handles any resident or family complaint about a discharge under POL-07.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on discharge, gives notices, requests Department exceptions, supports relocation, keeps the discharge tracking chart and exception records.
Identifies excludable conditions and advises on accommodations.
Deliver notices when assigned, assist with packing and transfer, and return property.
Receive notice, take part in planning, and may give 14 days' notice to leave.

documentation: Pre-admission screening showing excludable-condition review
Department exception requests and approvals
Record of aging-in-place accommodations attempted
30-day written discharge notices with receipt
Resident's 14-day notice and acknowledgment
Discharge tracking chart
Closure notice to the Department (60 days) and to residents
Receipt for property, funds and medications returned

policies.category: 8. The home's policies and procedures (items a through r)
policies.title: Records Policy
policies.applies_to: ALR (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and PCH (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600) – all staff, volunteers and contractors who create, use, store or destroy resident records
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps a complete, separate, secure and confidential record for every resident. The record must be available to authorized persons, kept for the required period and destroyed in a controlled way.
policies.policy: This policy meets 55 Pa. Code § 2600.254(b) (checklist item 8(r) – Records Policy) and its Chapter 2800 counterpart, §2800.254(b), the written record security policy. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate, on-site record for each resident that holds all 28 required content items listed in §2800.251. Records are kept locked when not in use. Only the people permitted by §2800.17 may see them. Without the resident's written consent, those people are the resident, the resident's designated person, staff providing services to the resident, DHS agents and the long-term care ombudsman. Records may also be released in an emergency or on a court order. Records are kept for 3 years after the resident's death or discharge, or until any audit or litigation has ended, whichever is later. When the retention period ends, records are destroyed in a confidential manner and the destruction is entered in a destruction log. If [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, it also follows 45 CFR Part 164. This policy is the written record security policy required by §2800.254(b).

definitions.definition: The separate, on-site file kept for one resident that contains the 28 content items required by §2800.251, including the contract, medical evaluation, assessments and support plan.
The person the resident has named in writing to act for the resident or to receive information about the resident.
A permanent log showing which resident records were destroyed, when, by what method and by whom.
The person assigned by the administrator to control access, filing, retention and destruction of records.

procedures: The administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], appoints a record custodian and a backup in writing. Their names are posted in the records room and listed in the staff list (ORG-01).
On the day of application, the custodian opens a separate record for each applicant or resident. The file is labeled with the resident's name, and no two residents' records are combined.
The custodian keeps a Record Content Checklist inside each file. It lists all 28 content items required by §2800.251, and the custodian marks each item as it is added, with the date and initials.

Staff add documents to the record as they are created. Admission documents are filed no later than the day after admission. Later documents (support plan updates, medical re-evaluations, incident reports) are filed within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days of creation.

Records are stored on-site at [ADDRESS] in a locked cabinet or locked room. Only the custodian, the administrator and designees named in writing hold keys or codes. Records are never left on desks, counters or in unlocked areas.

Electronic records, if used, are kept on a password-protected system with unique user IDs. Each user's access is limited to what the job requires, backups are made regularly, and the on-site record can be printed on request.
Staff may see only the records of residents they serve. Staff sign a confidentiality acknowledgment at hire (see POL-02).

Before releasing any record or information, the custodian checks the request against §2800.17. If the requester is the resident, the designated person, staff providing services, a DHS agent or the ombudsman, the custodian releases the record. For anyone else, the custodian first obtains the resident's written consent, unless there is an emergency or a court order.

In an emergency, such as a hospital transfer, staff send the information needed for care (medications, allergies, diagnoses, contacts, advance directives). They record what was sent, to whom and when.
For a court order, the administrator reviews the order and releases only what it requires. A copy of the order and of the released material is filed.
Each release is entered in a Record Access and Release Log that shows the date, the requester, what was released and the authority for release (consent, emergency, court order or regulator).
When a DHS inspector asks for records, the administrator or designee provides them promptly on-site. A staff member stays with the records and notes which records were reviewed.
Records are never removed from the home, except under court order or an emergency transfer. Staff do not take photographs of records or send them by personal email or text.

When a resident dies or is discharged, the custodian completes the record, writes the retention-end date on the file cover and moves the file to locked inactive storage. The retention-end date is 3 years after the death or discharge date.

If the home learns of an audit, investigation or litigation involving a resident, the custodian puts a hold on that record. The record is kept until the administrator confirms in writing that the matter has ended.
Each quarter, the custodian reviews inactive records and lists those past their retention-end date with no hold. The administrator approves the list in writing before any record is destroyed.

Approved records are destroyed confidentially by shredding or secure incineration, or by a contracted destruction vendor under a written confidentiality agreement. Electronic records are permanently erased in a way that prevents recovery.

The custodian enters each destruction in the destruction log (resident name or ID, discharge or death date, destruction date, method, person who performed it and witness). The log is kept permanently.

If a record is lost, stolen or seen by an unauthorized person, staff tell the administrator immediately. The administrator investigates, notifies the resident or designated person, and applies HIPAA breach rules if the home is a covered entity. Reporting follows POL-01 and corrective action is entered in the quality management plan (POL-03).
The administrator reviews this policy and the Record Content Checklist at least annually and after any change in regulations. Staff are trained on it at orientation and annually (PLAN-01).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and enforces this policy, appoints the custodian, approves destruction, and handles breaches and regulator requests.
Maintains each record and its checklist, controls keys and access, keeps the access and release log, tracks retention and keeps the destruction log.
Document accurately and on time, access only records of residents they serve, and return records to locked storage.
Keep resident information confidential and report any loss or improper disclosure at once.

documentation: Resident record with Record Content Checklist (28 items under §2800.251)
Record Access and Release Log
Written resident consents for release, and copies of court orders
Retention and Destruction Schedule with administrator approval
Destruction log
Staff confidentiality acknowledgments and records security training
Record custodian appointment

policies.category: 9. Special Care Unit (ALR) / Secured Dementia Care Unit (PCH) documentation, if applicable
policies.title: SCU Environmental Protection Policy and Lock Approvals
policies.applies_to: ALR special care unit and PCH secured dementia care unit (SDCU), if [AGENCY NAME] operates or plans one – administrator, maintenance and all SCU staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that any unit for residents with dementia has a safe, protective environment. Locks, alarms and other wandering-prevention measures must be approved before use, must never block safe evacuation, and must be documented for DHS.
policies.policy: This policy meets checklist item 9(b), the Environmental Protection Policy (55 Pa. Code § 2600.232(d); ALR counterpart §2800.232(d)), and checklist item 9(c), Lock Approvals (§ 2600.233(a)-(b); ALR counterpart §2800.233(a)-(b)). [AGENCY NAME] will not open or operate a special care unit (SCU) or secured dementia care unit (SDCU) until DHS has approved it. The home applies to DHS at least 60 days before opening the unit and pays the $150 special care designation fee under §2800.11. The unit's environment is designed to protect residents from hazards and to reduce wandering, and each measure is written in the environmental protection policy below. Every lock, alarm or other secured-exit device is used only after the approvals required by §2800.233(a)-(b) are obtained. All egress arrangements must satisfy the home's fire safety approval (PLT-01) and the egress and exit requirements of §§2800.121–2800.124. Egress routes stay unobstructed and exits stay available for evacuation. The home notifies the local fire department in writing, as required by those sections. Only licensed 'assisted living residences' may use that term; the home uses 'special care unit' or 'secured dementia care unit' only for a unit that DHS has approved. This policy applies only if the home operates an SCU or SDCU. If not, the home records 'Not applicable' on the checklist.

definitions.term: Special care unit (SCU) / secured dementia care unit (SDCU)
definitions.definition: A designated, DHS-approved unit, or the whole residence, that serves residents with Alzheimer's disease or other dementia and uses a secured environment. 'SCU' is the ALR term and 'SDCU' is the PCH term.
The written description of the physical features and practices used to keep SCU residents safe and to prevent unsafe wandering.
The written approval required by §2800.233(a)-(b) (§2600.233(a)-(b) for PCH) before a lock or secured-exit device is used.
The approval of the residence's fire safety and egress arrangements, kept under PLT-01.

procedures: Before any SCU or SDCU is planned, the administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], decides in writing whether the home will have one and which units or beds will be included. The decision is recorded on the floor plan (PLT-01).

The administrator submits the SCU application to DHS at least 60 days before the intended opening date and pays the $150 special care designation fee. The submission date, receipt and fee payment are filed in the licensing file (GOV-01).

The administrator writes the environmental protection policy for the unit. It describes the secured perimeter, door and exit controls, alarms, outdoor access, lighting, hazard control (for example chemicals, hot surfaces, stairs), and the wandering-prevention measures to be used.
The administrator lists every proposed lock, alarm or secured-exit device on a Lock and Secured-Exit Register by location, type, purpose, and who can release or override it.

Before installation, the administrator checks each proposed device against the fire safety approval and the egress requirements (§§2800.121–2800.124). Any device that would lock an egress route, block an exit or delay evacuation is changed before it is installed.
The administrator obtains every approval required by §2800.233(a)-(b) for each device. The administrator files the written approvals and confirms that none has expired or been limited by conditions.
No lock, alarm or secured-exit device is put into use until its approval is on file. The maintenance lead and administrator both initial the register to authorize activation.

The administrator confirms that two independent exits per floor remain available and unobstructed. For residents above or below grade with mobility needs, the home confirms that the required fire-safe area is available.

Staff are given the release method (key, code or button) for each secured door. Release devices are available to every staff person on duty in the unit at all times, and the method is covered in SCU training (SCU-02).
The administrator posts emergency procedures and floor diagrams as required for the home's size, and shows the secured-exit locations and release methods on them.
The home sends written notice to the local fire department about the home and the secured unit. A copy and the date sent are filed.

Staff check each secured door, alarm and release device daily. Maintenance tests them monthly. Results are entered in the Lock and Secured-Exit Inspection Log, and any failure is repaired immediately or the unit is staffed with extra supervision until repair.
Fire drills include the SCU on every shift and test the release of secured exits (SAF-04). Drill times, evacuation results and problems are recorded on the fire drill record (FRM-04).

Wandering-prevention measures are documented for each resident in the support plan (FRM-03), including individual risk, triggers, supervision level and what staff do if the resident tries to leave. Elopement response follows SAF-03.

If a lock fails, a resident exits unsafely, or a device is found unapproved, staff tell the administrator immediately. The administrator applies POL-01 for any reportable incident and enters corrective action in the quality management plan (POL-03).

Before any change to the unit's doors, locks, alarms, layout or perimeter, the administrator updates the environmental protection policy and obtains new approvals as required. Updates are dated and filed.
The administrator reviews this policy, the register and the approvals at least annually and when DHS inspection findings, regulations or the physical plant change.

responsibilities.duty: Applies to DHS, pays the fee, writes and updates the environmental protection policy, obtains and files lock approvals and signs off activation of every device.
Installs, tests and repairs devices as approved, keeps the inspection log and never installs a device that blocks egress.
Check secured doors and alarms each day, know the release methods and apply individual wandering-prevention measures.
Tracks failures, drill results and elopement events, and follows corrective actions.

documentation: SCU application, DHS correspondence and $150 fee receipt
Written environmental protection policy for the unit
Lock and Secured-Exit Register
Lock approvals under §2800.233(a)-(b)
Fire safety approval and egress documentation (PLT-01)
Written notice to the local fire department
Daily check and monthly inspection logs
Fire drill records that include the SCU
Resident wandering-prevention plans in support plans

policies.category: 9. Special Care Unit (ALR) / Secured Dementia Care Unit (PCH) documentation, if applicable
policies.title: SCU Training and Staffing
policies.applies_to: ALR special care unit and PCH secured dementia care unit (SDCU), if applicable – administrator and all staff, substitutes and volunteers who work in or support the unit
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who works in the special care unit is trained to serve residents with dementia, and that the unit is staffed so that every SCU resident receives the required direct care time.
policies.policy: This policy meets checklist item 9(d), SCU/SDCU Training (55 Pa. Code § 2600.236; ALR counterpart §2800.236), and checklist item 9(f), SCU/SDCU Staffing (§ 2600.238; ALR counterpart §2800.238). Staff who work in the unit complete 8 hours of SCU training initially and 8 hours annually, as required by §2800.236. The 4 hours of dementia-specific training within 30 days of hire and 2 hours annually required by §2800.69 for administrative, direct care, ancillary and substitute staff and volunteers apply in addition to SCU training and to other required training. The unit is staffed under §2800.238, and every SCU resident is scheduled for at least 2 hours per day of direct care time. Training records are kept for every person. No one works unsupervised in the unit until the initial SCU training required by §2800.236 is complete. This policy applies only if the home operates an SCU or SDCU.

definitions.definition: The 8 hours of special care unit training required by §2800.236 for staff who work in the unit.
The 8 hours of SCU training required each year under §2800.236.
The 4 hours required within 30 days of hire and 2 hours required each year under §2800.69, in addition to other required training.
Time staff spend providing assisted living services and supervision to residents, counted toward the daily hour requirement of §2800.238.

procedures: The administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], identifies every position that works in or supports the unit (direct care, nursing, activities, housekeeping, dietary, maintenance, administrative, substitutes and volunteers) and lists them on the SCU Training Matrix.

At hire or assignment, the administrator assigns the 4 hours of dementia-specific training (§2800.69), due within 30 days of hire, and the 8 hours of initial SCU training (§2800.236). Due dates are entered on the matrix.
A staff person new to the SCU does not work alone and does not count toward unit staffing until the initial SCU training is complete. Until then the person works beside a trained staff person.

SCU training content is chosen to match the SCU program (SCU-03) and covers the nature of dementia, communication, behavior and wandering, safe use of the secured environment (SCU-01), activities and resident rights. Training is delivered only by qualified trainers listed in the Training Plan (PLAN-01) or by approved outside providers.
Staff sign an attendance sheet for each session showing the date, the topic, the trainer and the hours. Certificates from outside trainers are collected and filed.

Each year, the administrator schedules the 8 hours of annual SCU training and the 2 hours of annual dementia-specific training before each person's anniversary date. The training matrix shows both sets of hours separately so that neither is counted twice.
Training hours for other required topics (for example first aid, CPR, fire safety) are tracked separately, since dementia and SCU hours are in addition to them (TRN-01).
Substitutes and volunteers who work in the SCU complete the same dementia-specific and SCU training before they work in the unit without supervision.

The administrator sets the unit's staffing pattern under §2800.238 and records it in the planned staffing pattern (STF-01). It states the number of staff by shift and shows how every SCU resident receives at least 2 hours per day of direct care time.

The shift supervisor checks staffing at the start of every shift against the pattern. If a call-off leaves the unit short, the supervisor calls a trained substitute from the on-call list and tells the administrator.

Each month, the administrator totals direct care hours provided in the SCU and compares them with the number of residents multiplied by 2 hours per day. The calculation is signed and filed. Shortfalls are corrected in the following schedule, and the cause is added to the quality management plan (POL-03).
A direct care staff person age 21 or older stays in the residence whenever any resident is present, and awake staff coverage follows STF-02.

The administrator keeps SCU training records for each person: training matrix, attendance sheets, certificates and trainer qualifications. Records are kept in the personnel file and available to DHS on inspection.
The administrator reviews the training matrix every month and reviews the staffing calculations each quarter. A resident's change in care needs triggers a review of staffing for the unit.
The administrator reviews this policy annually and when regulations, the SCU program or the unit's census change.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns and schedules training, sets the SCU staffing pattern, verifies the 2-hour-per-day rule each month and keeps training records.
Checks SCU staffing each shift, calls substitutes and makes sure untrained staff do not work alone in the unit.
Delivers or arranges the training, records attendance and hours, and provides certificates.
Complete the required training by the due dates and apply it in daily care.

documentation: SCU Training Matrix with due and completion dates
Attendance sheets and certificates for initial SCU (8 hours), annual SCU (8 hours) and dementia-specific training (4 hours initial, 2 hours annual)
Trainer qualifications
Planned SCU staffing pattern
Monthly SCU direct care hours calculation (2 hours per resident per day)
Daily shift staffing sheets
Personnel training files

policies.category: 9. Special Care Unit (ALR) / Secured Dementia Care Unit (PCH) documentation, if applicable
policies.title: SCU Program Information and General SCU Information
policies.applies_to: ALR special care unit and PCH secured dementia care unit (SDCU), if applicable – administrator, nursing, admissions and SCU activity staff
policies.purpose: To describe the SCU program and the general SCU information that the home provides to DHS and to residents and families. The program includes pre-admission cognitive screening, regular reassessment and a weekly activities program.
policies.policy: This policy meets checklist item 9(e), SCU/SDCU Program Information (§2600.237(a)(1)-(6); ALR counterpart §2800.237(a)(1)-(6)), and checklist item 9(g), General SCU/SDCU Information (§ 2600.239(a), (c)(1)-(22); ALR counterpart §2800.239(a), (c)(1)-(22)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written SCU program description that addresses each of the six elements listed in §2800.237(a)(1)-(6). The home prepares general SCU information that addresses §2800.239(a) and each of the 22 items in §2800.239(c)(1)-(22). Both documents are built item by item on an SCU Disclosure Checklist, so every numbered item is addressed and can be found. A resident is admitted to the unit only after a cognitive screening completed within 72 hours before admission, and is reassessed quarterly. The unit provides a weekly activities program. The same program and general information are provided at application to every prospective SCU resident and family. They are kept current. This policy applies only if the home operates an SCU or SDCU. The PCH secured dementia care unit rules are in §§2600.231–2600.239.

definitions.definition: The written description of the unit's program covering the six elements required by §2800.237(a)(1)-(6).
The written information required by §2800.239(a) and (c)(1)-(22) that the home gives to DHS, residents and families about the unit.
A structured screening of a resident's cognition, completed within 72 hours before admission to the unit, and repeated quarterly as reassessment.
The home's tracking form that lists every numbered item in §2800.237(a) and §2800.239 and shows where each is addressed.

procedures: The administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], builds the SCU Disclosure Checklist with one line for each of the six elements in §2800.237(a)(1)-(6), one line for §2800.239(a), and one line for each of the 22 items in §2800.239(c)(1)-(22).
The administrator and the nursing lead write the SCU program description so that each of the six elements is addressed in a labeled section. The checklist records the page or section for each.
The administrator prepares the general SCU information so that §2800.239(a) and each item in (c)(1)-(22) is addressed in a labeled section. The checklist records where each is located.
Before submitting to DHS, a second person (the nursing lead or consultant listed in CON-01) reads both documents against the checklist and signs that no numbered item has been left out.
The SCU program and general information are included in the application package for the unit (SCU-01), and copies are kept in the licensing file (GOV-01).

At first contact, admissions staff give each prospective SCU resident and family a copy of the SCU program and general information, together with the admission disclosures and contract (FRM-01). The date given is recorded in the resident file.

Within 72 hours before admission, a person qualified under the home's program completes a cognitive screening of the prospective resident. The result is signed, dated and placed in the resident record. Admission to the unit does not proceed without it.

If the screening, medical evaluation (FRM-02) or initial assessment shows that the unit cannot meet the person's needs, the administrator gives a written denial and refers the person elsewhere (AR-01).
The support plan (FRM-03) for each SCU resident states the resident's cognitive status, preferred routines, wandering risk and planned activities.

The nursing lead reassesses every SCU resident's cognition each quarter and whenever the resident's condition changes. The result is filed in the record and the support plan is updated. Changes in condition follow HC-01.

The activities coordinator posts and carries out a weekly activities program for the unit, with activities matched to residents' cognitive abilities and interests. Attendance and participation are noted on the activity log (DL-02).
If a resident no longer fits the unit, or the unit cannot meet the resident's needs, the administrator follows the discharge and transfer policy (POL-16).

The administrator reviews the program description, general information and checklist at least annually and whenever the unit changes. The updated documents are dated and re-issued to families on request and to DHS as required.
Staff are trained on the SCU program at orientation and annually (SCU-02).

responsibilities.duty: Writes and updates the SCU program and general information, keeps the checklist complete, and gives the information at application.
Completes or oversees cognitive screening within 72 hours before admission and quarterly reassessment, and updates support plans.
Deliver SCU information and disclosures to applicants and families and record the delivery date.
Plans and carries out the weekly SCU activities program and records participation.

documentation: SCU program description (§2800.237(a)(1)-(6))
General SCU information (§2800.239(a), (c)(1)-(22))
SCU Disclosure Checklist with second-reader sign-off
Cognitive screening within 72 hours before admission, and quarterly reassessments
Support plans for SCU residents
Weekly SCU activity schedules and logs
Record of delivery of SCU information to applicants

policies.title: Resident-Residence Contract and Admission Disclosures
policies.applies_to: ALR (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and PCH (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600) – administrator, admissions staff and business office
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives the required written disclosures at application and signs a compliant resident-residence contract that clearly states charges, notice periods, refunds and rights.
policies.policy: This policy and the attached form meet checklist item 10(a), Resident-Home Contract (55 Pa. Code § 2600.25(c)(1)-(13), § 2600.25(d) Statement of Policy, § 2600.25(e)-(f), and § 2600.109(a), (d)); the ALR counterparts are §2800.25 and §§2800.108–2800.109. The contract form has a section for each of the 13 items in §2600.25(c)(1)-(13). The form follows the Department's statement of policy in §2600.25(d) and addresses §2600.25(e)-(f). The pet provisions of §2600.109(a) and (d) are addressed in the pet section of the contract. A Contract Compliance Checklist lists each of these items and is completed for every contract. Under §2800.25 the contract is month-to-month, with 14 days' written notice by the resident and 30 days' written notice by the residence. It contains a fee schedule, refund terms and bed-hold charges, and any pet charges. Residents may rescind within 72 hours. No contract may require assignment of assets for life care. On application, the home gives the disclosures required by §2800.22(e): the list of non-waivable rights, the contract, the rules, the DHS-approved resident handbook, the costs of services and the core package, DHS contact information, how to access inspection reports, the number of ADA-compliant units and any waivers in effect. The contract is signed no later than 24 hours after admission (§2800.22), and the home's practice is to sign before move-in. Prepaid charges are refunded within 30 days of discharge, the personal needs allowance within 2 business days, and managed funds within 2 business days after the unit is cleared. An itemized account is given within 30 days. Refunds after a death follow the Elder Care Payment Restitution Act for residents aged 60 and over (§2800.28). Because residence charges are mostly private pay and Community HealthChoices generally does not cover PCH/ALR residence charges, the contract states plainly who pays and from what source (see POL-04).

definitions.definition: The written agreement between [AGENCY NAME] and the resident (or the resident's legal representative) that sets out services, charges, notice periods, refunds and rights.
The set of services and basics included in the base monthly charge, as described in the home's description of services (POL-15).
A charge, stated in the contract, for keeping a unit available while the resident is temporarily away.
The resident's right to cancel the contract within 72 hours of signing.
The list of resident rights that a resident cannot waive, provided at application (POL-05).

procedures: When a person applies, the admissions coordinator opens an admission file and records the date of application.

On the day of application, the coordinator gives the applicant and any representative the disclosure packet: non-waivable rights list, blank contract, residence rules, DHS-approved resident handbook, price list for services and the core package, DHS contact information (BHSL 717-783-3670; complaint line 1-877-401-8835), how to see inspection reports, the number of ADA-compliant units and any waivers in effect.

The applicant or representative signs a Disclosure Receipt that lists each item, and the signed receipt is filed. If the person cannot read English or has a disability, the coordinator provides language assistance or reads the documents aloud (RR-03).

The coordinator explains the contract, including the month-to-month term, 14-day resident notice and 30-day residence notice, the fee schedule, what is and is not in the core package, refund terms, bed-hold charges and any pet charges. The applicant may take the contract home to review.

The contract is prepared from the home's standard form and completed for the individual resident: unit, start date, monthly charge, services chosen and their costs, and source of payment. Medicaid and Community HealthChoices are not assumed to pay residence charges, and the contract says so.

The administrator checks the contract against the Contract Compliance Checklist, which covers §2600.25(c)(1)-(13), §2600.25(d), §2600.25(e)-(f) and §2600.109(a),(d), and the ALR requirements of §2800.25, and signs the checklist before the contract goes to the resident.

If the resident has a pet, the contract section on pets states the pet charges. Staff collect a current rabies certificate for each cat or dog and file it with the contract (POL-13). If pets are not allowed, the contract says so.
The contract states the 72-hour rescission right in plain print near the signature line. It contains no term that requires assigning the resident's assets for life care.

The contract states the refund terms: refund of prepaid charges within 30 days of discharge, the personal needs allowance within 2 business days, managed funds within 2 business days after the unit is cleared, an itemized account within 30 days, and death refunds under the Elder Care Payment Restitution Act for residents aged 60 and over.

Before admission, the administrator confirms that the medical evaluation (FRM-02) and initial assessment are complete and signs the certification that the home can meet the resident's needs (AR-01). If not, the administrator issues a written denial and referral and no contract is signed.

The resident or representative and an authorized agent of the home sign and date the contract. The resident receives a complete copy at signing. The contract is signed before move-in or, at the latest, within 24 hours after admission.

The coordinator starts the 72-hour rescission period at signing and records the end time. If the resident rescinds, the administrator processes the refund under the refund terms in the contract (RR-01).
The original contract is filed in the resident record (POL-17). The business office sets up the charges in the billing system exactly as written in the contract.

Any change to charges or services is made only by written notice and written amendment to the contract, signed by the resident or representative and the home, and a copy is given to the resident. The notice period follows the contract.
When a resident gives or receives notice of discharge, the administrator records the notice date, the planned discharge date and the refund due date, and follows POL-16 and RR-01.

At discharge or death, the business office prepares the itemized account of charges and refunds within 30 days, sends refunds on the deadlines in the contract, and files proof of mailing in the record.
The administrator reviews the contract form and disclosure packet each year and after any regulation, fee or DHS-approved handbook change. A new version is dated, and staff are trained on it.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the contract form, checks each contract, certifies admission and makes sure refunds are on time.
Provides disclosures at application, explains and prepares the contract, and tracks the 72-hour rescission period.
Applies charges as written, prepares itemized accounts and issues refunds on the deadlines.
Reviews and signs the contract and may rescind within 72 hours.

Signed Disclosure Receipt for the application packet
DHS-approved resident handbook edition and rights list given
Fee schedule, core package and service price list
Pet agreement and rabies certificates, if applicable
Rescission period record
Admission certification and any written denial and referral
Notice of discharge, itemized account and refund proof

policies.title: Resident Medical Evaluation and Health Care Form
policies.applies_to: ALR (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and PCH (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600) – administrator, admissions staff, nursing and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident has a current medical evaluation on the DHS form, completed by an authorized health professional before admission and updated regularly. The evaluation gives staff the health information needed to care for the resident safely.
policies.policy: This policy and the attached form meet checklist item 10(d), Resident medical evaluation and health care (55 Pa. Code § 2600.141; ALR counterpart §2800.141). [AGENCY NAME] uses the DHS-prescribed medical evaluation form. A physician, physician assistant (PA) or certified registered nurse practitioner (CRNP) must complete it. The form covers diagnosis, allergies, medications, mobility needs and a tuberculosis (TB) test within the past 2 years, or a TB test obtained within 15 days of admission. The evaluation must be completed within 60 days before admission (§2800.22(a)-(c)). It is repeated at least annually and whenever the resident's medical condition changes. A resident is not admitted without a completed evaluation, and the home must certify before admission that it can meet the resident's needs.

definitions.definition: The health assessment of a resident completed on the DHS form by a physician, PA or CRNP under §2800.141.
A tuberculosis test result recorded on the evaluation, dated within 2 years before the evaluation or obtained within 15 days of admission.
A new diagnosis, a significant decline or improvement, hospitalization or any other change that affects the resident's care needs and requires a new evaluation.
The repeat medical evaluation required at least once every year.

procedures: At application, the admissions coordinator gives the applicant the current DHS-prescribed medical evaluation form and asks that it be completed by the applicant's physician, PA or CRNP. The coordinator explains that it must be completed within 60 days before admission.

Staff check that the form being used is the current version on the DHS site. The forms library (FRM-04) keeps only the current version, and the administrator replaces it whenever DHS issues a new one.

When the form comes back, the nursing lead reviews it the same day. The nursing lead confirms that it is on the DHS form, signed and dated by a physician, PA or CRNP, and that the provider's credential is shown.

The nursing lead checks that the form states diagnosis, allergies, medications, mobility needs, and a TB test result. The TB test must be dated within 2 years before the evaluation, or the resident must be tested within 15 days of admission.

The nursing lead confirms the evaluation date is within 60 days before the planned admission date. If it is older, staff ask the applicant for a new evaluation and the admission date is moved until one is received.

If the form is incomplete, illegible or inconsistent with the initial assessment, the nursing lead calls the provider's office, records the call and obtains a corrected form. No admission occurs until the problem is fixed.

If the TB test is to be obtained after admission, staff record the due date (15 days after admission) on the admission checklist. The nursing lead follows up and files the result. A positive result is handled under SAF-05 and the provider's instructions.

The administrator uses the evaluation, the initial assessment (FRM-03) and the pre-admission screening to decide whether the home can meet the resident's needs. The administrator signs the certification before admission (AR-01). If the needs cannot be met, the administrator gives a written denial and referral and does not admit the person.

The signed evaluation is filed in the resident record (POL-17). Allergies, diagnoses and medication information are transferred to the medication administration record and the support plan within 24 hours of admission (POL-14).
The nursing lead enters the next annual evaluation due date in the resident tracking calendar at admission. Staff are reminded at 60 days and again at 30 days before the due date.

The resident or representative arranges for the annual evaluation by the resident's physician, PA or CRNP, and staff assist with the appointment and transportation if requested (DL-02). The completed form is filed within 5 business days after the visit.

When the resident has a change in medical condition, a hospitalization or a significant change in medications, direct care staff tell the nursing lead the same day (HC-01). The nursing lead arranges a new medical evaluation on the DHS form and, if the support plan is affected, a reassessment (FRM-03).
Staff compare each new evaluation with the current support plan and medication orders within 2 business days. Differences are resolved with the provider and the support plan is updated.

The nursing lead audits the resident records each quarter to confirm that each has a current evaluation, and reports late or missing evaluations to the administrator. Findings go into the quality management plan (POL-03).
Evaluations are confidential and are released only as allowed by POL-02 and POL-17. The administrator reviews this policy annually.

responsibilities.duty: Certifies before admission that needs can be met, ensures the form is current and ensures no resident is admitted without a compliant evaluation.
Reviews each evaluation for completeness, tracks TB tests and annual due dates, arranges re-evaluations and audits records quarterly.
Provides the form at application, checks dates and moves the admission date if needed.
Completes and signs the DHS evaluation form.

documentation: Completed DHS medical evaluation form in each resident record
TB test result and date
Admission certification (AR-01)
Record of calls to providers and corrected forms
Annual evaluation tracking calendar
Quarterly record audit results
Current-version DHS form in the forms library (FRM-04)

policies.title: Initial Assessment, Additional Assessments and Support Plan Forms
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800) and Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600); all residents, including residents of a special care unit if one is approved
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] uses standard, complete forms to screen applicants, assess residents and write support plans. These forms show that the residence can meet each resident's needs before admission and keeps meeting them afterward.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses the written forms listed below for every applicant and resident. Each form is kept in the controlled forms library (FRM-04). This policy meets 55 Pa. Code §2600.224(a) (item 10(e) – Preadmission Screening Form), 55 Pa. Code §2600.225(b) (item 10(f) – Assessment Form) and 55 Pa. Code §2600.227(b) (item 10(g) – Support Plan Form). In the assisted living residence, the same forms serve as the initial assessment and preliminary support plan (§2800.224), the annual and significant-change reassessment (§2800.225) and the final support plan (§2800.227). Admission is conditioned on certification that the residence can meet the applicant's needs (§2800.22). If it cannot, [AGENCY NAME] gives a written denial and refers the applicant elsewhere. The initial assessment is completed within the 30 days before admission and the final support plan within 30 days after admission. For ALR residents, the medical evaluation (FRM-02) is dated within 60 days before admission. Assessments and preliminary support plans are completed only by a registered nurse, a licensed practical nurse working under a registered nurse, the administrator, or the administrator's trained designee. The final support plan is reviewed at least quarterly, signed, and given to the resident. If a special care unit is approved, the forms include the cognitive screening required by §§2800.231–2800.239.

definitions.definition: The form used before admission to decide whether the applicant is appropriate for the home and whether the home can meet the applicant's needs. In the PCH it is the form required by §2600.224. In the ALR it is built into the initial assessment form.

The standard form used to evaluate a resident's physical, medical, cognitive, psychosocial, functional and mobility needs. It is used for the initial assessment, the annual reassessment and any reassessment after a significant change.
The written plan listing the services and supports the resident will receive, who provides them, and how often. It starts as a preliminary plan and becomes the final support plan.
A change in the resident's physical, mental, functional or mobility condition that is major, lasting, or likely to affect the services the resident needs.
A resident's inability to move without help, including inability to evacuate unassisted, which DHS must be notified of.
A staff person named in writing by the administrator who has completed the required training to complete assessments and plans.

procedures: The administrator keeps the master versions of the Preadmission Screening Form, Assessment Form and Support Plan Form in the forms library (FRM-04). Each carries a version date and is reviewed at least annually.

When an inquiry becomes a serious application, the administrator or designee opens an admission file and completes the Preadmission Screening Form (AR-01). The screening covers the applicant's care needs, behaviors, medications, mobility, evacuation ability and personal goals.
The administrator or designee compares the screening results with the residence's description of services (POL-15), staffing (STF-01) and admission and retention limits (POL-16).
For ALR applicants, the applicant provides the physician-completed medical evaluation (FRM-02) dated within 60 days before admission. It is placed in the file before the assessment is finalized.

A registered nurse, a licensed practical nurse working under a registered nurse, the administrator, or a trained designee completes the Initial Assessment within the 30 days before admission. The assessor signs and dates the form.
The same assessor drafts the Preliminary Support Plan from the assessment, the medical evaluation and the applicant's and designated person's input.

For a prospective special care unit resident, staff also complete the cognitive screening within 72 hours before admission (SCU-03). The result is attached to the assessment and used to decide placement.

Before admission, the administrator certifies in writing, on the form, that the residence can meet the applicant's needs. If it cannot, the administrator gives the applicant a written denial within 24 hours of the decision, states the reasons, and refers the applicant to other options (AR-01).
The administrator or designee tells DHS about any resident with mobility needs, as required by the assessment and support plan rules, and records the date and method of notice in the resident's file.
On admission, the preliminary support plan takes effect. The resident or designated person receives a copy and staff review it with them in a language or mode they understand (RR-03).

Within 30 days after admission, the assessor, the resident and the designated person finish the final support plan. The resident or designated person signs it, and the resident receives a copy. The date given is written on the plan.
The administrator or designee reassesses each resident at least once every 12 months, using the Assessment Form. The next due date is entered in the tracking log when the assessment is signed.
Staff request a reassessment within 5 days of any significant change, including a fall with injury, hospitalization, new diagnosis, behavior change, weight change or new mobility limit (HC-01).
Within 30 days after each reassessment, staff update the support plan. They update it sooner when a need changes immediately.

The support plan is reviewed with the resident at least quarterly. The reviewer records the date, the changes made and the signatures. For special care unit residents, the cognitive screening is repeated quarterly and attached to the review.
Direct care staff are told about changes to a resident's support plan. They sign or initial a read-and-understood sheet before they work with that resident.

Superseded versions of the assessment and support plan stay in the resident's record under the Records Policy (POL-17). The administrator audits a sample of files each quarter as part of the Quality Management Plan (POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Keeps forms current, certifies whether needs can be met, signs denials, notifies DHS of mobility needs, and audits files.

responsibilities.role: Registered Nurse or LPN under an RN
responsibilities.duty: Completes assessments and preliminary support plans when assigned, and reassesses after significant change.
Completes assessments and plans only after the required training and written appointment by the administrator.
Follow the current support plan and report changes in condition to the supervisor or nurse the same shift.
Takes part in the screening, assessment and plan meetings, and signs the final plan.
