policies.title: Nursing Services, Change of Condition and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800); administrator, nurses, designee, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure a licensed nurse is available at all times, that changes in a resident's condition are recognized, reported and acted on promptly, and that residents who need emergency or hospital care are transferred safely with their information.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] ensures that a licensed nurse is available or on call at all times (55 Pa. Code §2800.60). Staffing is based on residents' assessed needs, and the stated staffing levels are only a minimum. The residence helps residents secure medical care, documents refusals and efforts to obtain consent, and sends emergency data, including advance directives and DNR orders, with a resident who is transferred (§§2800.142–2800.143). The residence repeats the resident's medical evaluation at least annually and whenever the resident's medical condition changes (§2800.141). The residence reassesses the resident annually and when a significant change occurs, and updates the support plan (§§2800.224–2800.227). The final support plan is reviewed quarterly, signed and given to the resident. Staff notify the physician and designated person of any change in condition. A resident's death, a hospital-level injury and an unexplained absence are reportable to the Department within 24 hours (see POL-01).

definitions.definition: A registered nurse or licensed practical nurse licensed in Pennsylvania. An LPN works under the direction of an RN for assessments.
Reachable by phone at all times and able to give direction, and to come to the residence when needed.
A change in a resident's physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional status that is not expected to be short-term or that affects the services the resident needs.
The person named by the resident to be contacted about the resident's condition.
The information sent with the resident: face sheet, diagnoses, allergies, medication list, physician, designated person, advance directive and DNR order.

procedures: The administrator keeps a nurse roster showing at all times the name and phone number of the licensed nurse on duty or on call. The roster is posted at the staff station and given to all direct care staff, and any gap is corrected immediately.

The administrator reviews staffing against residents' assessed needs at least quarterly and whenever a resident's needs change. Staff hours are added if needs exceed the minimums (see STF-01 and STF-02).

All direct care staff are trained at orientation on recognizing and reporting changes in condition, such as new confusion, fall, poor intake, fever, chest pain, breathing difficulty, change in skin, pain, new behavior or refusal of care.
A staff person who notices a change tells the nurse, or the on-call nurse if no nurse is on site, immediately, and records the observation in the resident's daily notes with date, time and signature.

In an emergency, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, stroke signs, serious injury or heavy bleeding, staff call 911 first, then notify the nurse and administrator. Staff follow the emergency medical plan (POL-12).
Staff send with the resident, or immediately after if urgent, the emergency data, including the advance directive and DNR order. A staff person tells the ambulance crew the resident's code status.

For a non-emergency change, the nurse evaluates the resident the same day, or directs staff by phone and arranges an in-person evaluation promptly. The nurse contacts the resident's physician, PA or CRNP for orders and records the contact.

Staff help the resident make and keep medical appointments and arrange transportation (see DL-02). If a resident refuses care, staff document the refusal, the efforts to explain the risk and obtain consent, and notify the physician and, with the resident's agreement, the designated person (see RR-02).

Staff or the nurse notify the designated person of any significant change, injury, hospital transfer, new medication or serious refusal as soon as possible, and no later than the same day, and record the time and person told.

The nurse decides whether the change is a significant change. If so, the nurse or other qualified assessor reassesses the resident, and the support plan is updated and signed, and a copy is given to the resident (FRM-03).

The nurse checks whether the change makes the resident's condition one that is excluded, such as a pressure ulcer that is Stage III or IV, a need for continuous IV fluids, or a need for 24-hour skilled nursing. If so, the nurse tells the administrator at once and the administrator follows POL-16.

If the resident's medical condition has changed, the nurse or designee asks the resident's physician, PA or CRNP to update the medical evaluation on the DHS form (FRM-02). The annual repeat of the medical evaluation is scheduled by the designee at least 30 days before it is due.
If a resident has an unexplained absence, a hospital-level injury or dies, the administrator reports the incident to the Department within 24 hours and follows POL-01 and, for absence, SAF-03.

The nurse or designee records the hospital transfer, including the time, reason, who was notified, who accompanied the resident, the hospital, and what documents were sent, in the resident's record on the same shift.

Staff or the nurse call the hospital within 24 hours to check on status and to share information. The administrator or nurse stays in contact with the hospital and the designated person about discharge plans.

Before the resident returns, the nurse reviews the discharge orders, medication changes, and care needs. The nurse conducts a reassessment on return, and the administrator confirms that the residence can still meet the resident's needs and that no excludable condition exists.
Medication orders from the hospital are reconciled by the nurse before the next medication pass (see POL-14). Support plan changes and new service needs are recorded and explained to the resident.
The nurse reports significant changes, transfers and reportable incidents to the quality management committee quarterly (POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure a licensed nurse is available or on call at all times, adjust staffing to needs, file reportable incident notices within 24 hours, and decide on retention.
Evaluate changes in condition, contact physicians, direct care, complete or oversee reassessment, reconcile medications and document.
Observe and report changes at once, call 911 in an emergency, and send emergency data with the resident.
Notify designated persons, schedule medical evaluations and appointments, and keep records.

Daily notes and change-of-condition notes
Physician and designated person contact records
Reassessment and updated support plan, signed and copy given to the resident
Updated medical evaluation (DHS form)
Emergency data sheet and hospital transfer record
Refusal of care documentation
Reportable incident reports (POL-01)

policies.title: Hospice, Home Health Coordination and Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800); administrator, nurse, designee, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To allow residents to receive hospice care in the residence, to coordinate outside home health and hospice providers with the residence's own services, and to handle a resident's death with dignity, timely reporting and prompt return of property and funds.
policies.policy: Hospice care and services licensed by the Department of Health may be provided to a resident in [AGENCY NAME] (55 Pa. Code §2800.29). The residence works with the resident's chosen hospice or home health provider and ensures that the resident's support plan reflects all services given. The residence does not admit or keep a resident whose needs it cannot meet, or who has an excludable condition, unless DHS grants an exception (see AR-01 and POL-16). A resident's death is a reportable incident and is reported to the Department within 24 hours (§2800.16). Refunds at the end of a resident's stay follow §2800.28: prepaid charges are refunded within 30 days, the personal needs allowance within 2 business days, and managed funds within 2 business days of the unit being cleared, with an itemized account within 30 days. Refunds after a death for a resident age 60 or older follow the Elder Care Payment Restitution Act. The residence returns the resident's personal property to the legally authorized person with a signed inventory.

definitions.definition: A program licensed by the Pennsylvania Department of Health that provides comfort-focused care for people with a terminal illness and support for their families.
An outside licensed agency that provides skilled nursing or therapy services to a resident in the residence.
An incident or condition listed in §2800.16, including death, that must be reported to the Department.
The executor, administrator of the estate, agent under power of attorney as permitted after death, or other person entitled by law to receive property and funds.
The portion of a resident's income set aside for the resident's personal use, held or managed under RR-01.

procedures: When a resident or designated person asks about hospice, the nurse or designee gives information about hospice agencies licensed by the Department of Health and does not recommend one agency over another. The resident chooses the provider.

The administrator or nurse verifies that the agency is licensed by the Department of Health and obtains a copy of its license and a service agreement describing who provides each service and who to call after hours.

The nurse meets with the hospice or home health nurse to share the support plan and medication list. The hospice plan of care is added to the resident's record and the support plan is updated to show the services the residence and the outside provider each give.

The administrator confirms that the residence can continue to meet the resident's needs with hospice support. If the resident develops an excludable condition or needs 24-hour skilled nursing, the administrator follows AR-01 and POL-16 and requests a DHS exception where appropriate, or begins discharge planning with the resident.
Staff ask the resident about wishes for comfort, spiritual care, visitors and family involvement. Staff honor advance directives and DNR orders (RR-02) and make sure the DNR is readily available.

The nurse and hospice staff agree on medication management, including who gives and stores hospice medications, in line with POL-14. Hospice medications are stored in the same way as other residents' medications and are disposed of under POL-14.
Visitors are welcome at any time. Staff allow family to stay with a dying resident and help arrange privacy.

When a resident dies in the residence, the staff person calls the nurse, the hospice agency if enrolled, or 911 if not enrolled in hospice and no DNR is present, and tells the administrator immediately. Staff follow the DNR order.

The nurse or administrator notifies the physician, the designated person and the legally authorized person as soon as possible. They contact the funeral home chosen by the family or the resident's pre-arrangement.

The administrator reports the death to the Department within 24 hours as a reportable incident (see POL-01), by [REPORTING METHOD AND BHSL REGIONAL PHONE], and files any follow-up report required by POL-01. If the death was unexpected or suspicious, the administrator also follows SAF-01.
Staff protect the privacy and dignity of the deceased and of other residents. The administrator tells other residents in a sensitive way and offers support.
The nurse or designee records the death in the resident's record, including the time found, who was notified and when, the person who confirmed the death, and the funeral home that took the body.
The administrator or designee prepares a written inventory of the resident's personal property with a second staff person, and secures the unit.

The administrator releases the property to the legally authorized person on signed receipt. Managed funds and the personal needs allowance are returned within 2 business days of the unit being cleared (§2800.28).

The administrator calculates refunds. Prepaid charges are refunded within 30 days, and an itemized account of charges and credits is given within 30 days. For a resident age 60 or older, the refund is handled as required by the Elder Care Payment Restitution Act. The refund goes to the person legally entitled to it.
The administrator removes the resident from the census, updates the capacity records, and arranges cleaning and inspection of the unit before it is reassigned.
The administrator reviews each death at the next quality management meeting (POL-03) to look for prevention opportunities and to confirm that the reporting and refund deadlines were met.

responsibilities.duty: Report the death within 24 hours, approve hospice arrangements, manage refunds and property return, and keep records.
Coordinate with hospice and home health, update the support plan, handle notifications and document the death.
Provide comfort care, follow the DNR and call the nurse and administrator immediately.
Complete the property inventory, notify contacts and prepare the itemized account.

Hospice plan of care and updated support plan
Death note with notifications
Reportable incident report to the Department

policies.title: Falls Prevention and Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800); administrator, nurse, direct care staff, maintenance staff
policies.purpose: To reduce falls and pressure injuries through assessment, support plans, staff training and environmental safety, and to make sure bedside rails and other safety devices are used only as the regulations allow.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] works to prevent falls and skin breakdown through assessment and individualized support plans (55 Pa. Code §§2800.224–2800.227). All direct care staff receive annual training on falls prevention as part of their annual training under §2800.65. The residence does not admit or keep a resident with an unhealed Stage III or IV pressure ulcer unless DHS grants an exception (§2800.229). The residence uses positive interventions and does not use prohibited restraints, seclusion or aversive conditioning (§§2800.201–2800.203). Bedside rails are used only if the resident can operate them, only half-length rails are used, and the assessment and the resident's consent are documented. A fall or other event that results in an injury needing hospital-level care is reportable to the Department (see POL-01).

definitions.definition: An unplanned descent to the floor or other lower surface, with or without injury, including a resident found on the floor.
Localized damage to skin or underlying tissue from pressure or friction, staged I through IV by depth.
A rail covering about half the length of the bed, used as a mobility aid and not to confine the resident.
Any physical, mechanical or chemical means that restricts a resident's movement or behavior. Restraints are prohibited.
An injury that requires treatment at a hospital emergency department or inpatient care.

procedures: At admission and at least annually, and after any significant change, a qualified assessor (see FRM-03) assesses each resident's fall risk, mobility, balance, vision, continence, medication effects, cognition and skin condition.

The support plan lists specific fall and skin interventions for each resident, such as assistance with transfers, footwear, call devices, toileting schedule, repositioning, nutrition and hydration, and an assistive device. Plans are reviewed quarterly.
The nurse reviews each resident's medications with the physician or pharmacist when the resident falls repeatedly or has a change in condition, to look for medications that raise fall risk.

The administrator trains all direct care staff on falls prevention and skin care at orientation and again every year as part of the annual training, and keeps the training records (see TRN-01 and PLAN-01).

Maintenance staff inspect common areas and resident units at least weekly for hazards such as loose rugs, spills, poor lighting, clutter, broken handrails and uneven flooring, and fix them promptly. Hazards that cannot be fixed at once are blocked off and reported to the administrator.
Staff encourage safe activity, such as walking and exercise programs, and make sure residents have their glasses, hearing aids and walkers within reach.
Staff check skin during bathing and dressing. They report any redness that does not fade, blister, open area, bruise or swelling to the nurse the same day.

The nurse examines the area, stages any pressure injury, notifies the physician, PA or CRNP, and the designated person, and records the finding. Treatment follows the practitioner's orders, and the support plan is updated.

If a resident has or develops a pressure ulcer that is Stage III or IV and not healed, the nurse tells the administrator immediately. The administrator does not retain the resident unless DHS has granted an exception. The administrator applies POL-16 and asks DHS for an exception if appropriate, or arranges safe transfer or discharge with the resident and designated person.

When a resident falls, staff do not move the resident until the nurse or on-call nurse has been told. Staff call 911 if the resident is unresponsive, has severe pain, a suspected fracture, a head injury or bleeding that does not stop, and otherwise stay with the resident until the nurse evaluates.
The nurse evaluates the resident, contacts the physician as needed, and notifies the designated person. Staff monitor the resident per the nurse's direction after any head strike or unwitnessed fall.

Staff complete a fall report on the same shift, with the time, place, circumstances, injuries, notifications and contributing factors. The nurse reviews the report within 24 hours and updates the support plan.
If the injury needs hospital-level treatment, the administrator reports the incident to the Department within 24 hours under POL-01 and follows HC-01 for the hospital transfer.

Bedside rails are not used as a restraint. A rail is installed only if the resident can operate it, a qualified assessor documents the assessment and the physician or nurse approves, and the resident gives informed consent in writing. Only half-length rails are used.

The nurse reviews each rail at least quarterly and with any change in condition. The rail is removed if the resident can no longer operate it or no longer consents. The residence never uses full-length rails, lap belts, geri-chairs, locked tray tables or medications to restrict movement (see SAF-02).

The administrator reviews fall and pressure injury trends monthly, looking at time, place, and resident, and brings the findings to the quality management committee (POL-03) with any corrective action.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure training, environmental safety and compliance with exclusion rules, report hospital-level injuries, and review trends.
Assess fall and skin risk, stage wounds, notify physicians and families, review rails and update support plans.
Follow support plan interventions, check skin, report changes, and complete fall reports.
Inspect for and repair hazards.

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors and consultants of [AGENCY NAME] at the Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800). The same standard is adopted for any Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect, exploitation and abandonment, and to make sure every suspicion is reported immediately and handled as the Older Adult Protective Services Act (OAPSA) and the Department of Human Services (DHS) require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment of any resident. Under 55 Pa. Code §2800.15, any employee, volunteer or contractor who suspects abuse must report it immediately under OAPSA and 6 Pa. Code §§15.21–15.27. No staff member may wait for approval from a supervisor before making a report. When the allegation is against a staff person, the Administrator or designee must immediately supervise that person or suspend the person from duty, notify DHS immediately, and notify the resident and the resident's designated person. Hiring, criminal history checks and retention of staff follow OAPSA, 6 Pa. Code Ch. 15 and the Department of Aging's OAPSA hiring policy as required by 55 Pa. Code §§2800.51–2800.52 (see CHK-01). Direct care staff receive OAPSA/abuse-reporting training annually. No one will be retaliated against for reporting in good faith. This policy is also part of the reportable incident system in POL-01.

definitions.definition: Intentional infliction of physical, emotional or sexual harm, or willful deprivation of goods or services necessary to maintain physical or mental health, as defined by OAPSA and 6 Pa. Code Ch. 15.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medication or services a resident needs to avoid physical or psychological harm.
Improper use of a resident's funds, property or resources for another person's benefit, including misuse of resident funds.
The person the resident has named in the admission documents to be notified of incidents and changes in condition.
Any employee or administrator who has reasonable cause to suspect that a resident is a victim of abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment. Under OAPSA these staff must report.

procedures: Pre-employment: The Administrator completes all criminal history checks and hiring-eligibility review under OAPSA before a person has unsupervised contact with residents, and documents the results in the personnel file (see CHK-01).

Orientation: Before working with residents, every new staff person is trained on this policy, on how to recognize abuse, neglect and exploitation, and on the reporting steps below. The training is logged on the training record (see PLAN-01).
Annual training: Each direct care staff person completes OAPSA/abuse-prevention training every year. The Administrator tracks due dates and documents completion.

Prevention: Supervisors observe staff-resident interactions each shift and look for warning signs, such as unexplained bruises, fear of a particular person, withdrawal, missing funds or property, and poor hygiene. They record concerns on the shift report.

Any staff person who sees, hears of or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately protects the resident from further harm and notifies the Administrator or designee on duty. The staff person does not investigate on their own.

Immediately, and without waiting for the Administrator, the staff person or the Administrator makes the report required by OAPSA and 6 Pa. Code §§15.21–15.27 to [AREA AGENCY ON AGING PHONE] and/or the statewide protective services line [PROTECTIVE SERVICES HOTLINE]. Where a crime is suspected, the report also goes to [LOCAL POLICE PHONE] or 911.

If the allegation involves a staff person, the Administrator or designee immediately removes that person from resident contact. The person is either closely supervised or suspended from duty, based on the seriousness of the allegation. The decision and time are recorded.

The Administrator notifies DHS/BHSL immediately of an allegation involving a staff person. The call goes to the regional BHSL office at [REGIONAL BHSL OFFICE PHONE] (headquarters 717-783-3670). The Administrator then files the written report as set out in POL-01.

The Administrator or designee notifies the resident and the resident's designated person of the allegation and of the steps being taken, promptly and in a manner the resident can understand. Time, person contacted and content are documented.

The Administrator arranges any needed medical evaluation or treatment, and nursing assessment of the resident, and preserves evidence (clothing, records, schedules, video if any). Staff do not alter or discard anything related to the incident.

The Administrator conducts an internal fact-finding review in cooperation with the Area Agency on Aging, police and DHS. Staff interviews are kept confidential. The review is documented without interfering with any outside investigation.

A staff person under investigation does not return to resident contact until the Administrator has determined, in light of the outside investigation and OAPSA requirements, that the resident will be safe. Staff found to have committed abuse are removed, and the facts are reported as the law requires.

The Administrator reviews the resident's support plan and living arrangements, adds protective measures, and offers the resident counseling or other follow-up support. Changes are recorded in the support plan (see FRM-03).

The Administrator records each incident in the reportable incident log and the Quality Management Plan review (see POL-01 and POL-03). The log is reviewed at least quarterly for patterns involving staff, shifts, locations or residents.
Retaliation against a resident or staff person who reports in good faith is prohibited. Any retaliation is itself treated as a rights violation and results in discipline up to termination.
Residents and families are told how to report abuse or file a complaint, including the complaint hotline posted in the residence (see POL-05 and POL-07).

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately; protect the resident; cooperate with investigations.
Make or confirm all reports, remove or supervise accused staff, notify DHS, the resident and the designated person, ensure training, and keep the records.
Perform the Administrator's duties on reporting, protection and notification when the Administrator is not present.
Assess the resident for injury and decline, and document findings.
Review incidents for trends and recommend corrective action.

policies.title: Restraints, Safe Management Techniques and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff who provide direct care or supervision, and all residents of the Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800). The same standard is adopted for any Personal Care Home (Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure staff respond to resident behavior with positive interventions, that prohibited restraints and restrictive practices are never used, and that bedside rails are used only as permitted.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses positive interventions to support residents whose behavior may be challenging (55 Pa. Code §2800.201). Seclusion, aversive conditioning, pressure points, and chemical, mechanical and manual restraints are prohibited and are never used (55 Pa. Code §2800.202). Bedside rails are used only if the resident can operate them. Only half-length rails are permitted, and only after a documented assessment and the resident's documented consent (55 Pa. Code §2800.203). Staff are trained in safe management techniques within 40 working hours of hire. Any use or suspected use of a prohibited practice is reported as a possible rights violation and, where applicable, as abuse under SAF-01 and POL-01.

definitions.definition: A non-physical approach that prevents or de-escalates behavior, such as redirection, offering choices, addressing unmet needs, reducing noise or stimulation, or changing the environment or routine.
A drug or medication used to control behavior or restrict freedom of movement when it is not a standard treatment for the resident's medical condition.

A device or material that restricts a resident's movement or access to their own body, such as belts, wrist ties, geriatric chairs with trays that cannot be removed by the resident, or sheets tucked so that the resident cannot rise.
Holding or physically restricting a resident's body so that the resident cannot move freely.
Placing or confining a resident alone in a room or area from which the resident cannot leave or is prevented from leaving.
Use of painful, noxious or unpleasant stimuli to change or control behavior.
A rail attached to a bed. Only half-length rails that the resident can operate are permitted.

procedures: Within 40 working hours of hire, and before working alone with residents, each direct care staff person is trained in safe management techniques and positive interventions. Training is recorded in the training file (see TRN-01 and PLAN-01).
Each resident's behavior triggers, preferences and effective calming approaches are written in the support plan and kept where all shifts can see them (see FRM-03).
When a resident becomes agitated, staff first look for causes such as pain, hunger, toileting needs, infection, medication effects, noise, fear or confusion, and address them.

Staff use positive interventions, such as a calm voice, redirection, offering a walk, music, a quiet space the resident is free to leave, or one-to-one company. Staff do not argue with or threaten the resident.

If a resident is in danger of harming self or others, staff move others out of harm's way, keep a safe distance and call the Administrator or designee. If there is imminent danger, staff call 911. Staff never use seclusion, pressure points, holds or restraints.

Staff never give or request medication to control behavior unless a physician has prescribed it for a diagnosed condition, with the resident's informed consent. Any medication change that follows a behavior incident is reviewed by the nurse and physician (see POL-14 and HC-01).
Staff never lock a resident in a room, tie or hold a resident in a chair or bed, use a sheet or garment to restrict movement, or take away mobility aids to keep the resident from moving.

Bedside rails: before any rail is installed, the licensed nurse or Administrator completes a documented assessment of the resident's ability to operate the rail, the risk of entrapment and fall, and alternatives that were tried.

Only half-length rails may be installed. Rails are installed only if the resident can operate them and the resident or legal representative gives documented consent (see RR-02). A rail the resident cannot operate is removed.
The nurse or Administrator checks each rail's fit, condition and entrapment risk at the time of installation and at least with each support plan review, and records it.

The designee on duty reports any use or suspected use of a prohibited practice to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator removes the staff person from resident contact, makes the SAF-01 report and the POL-01 incident report, and notifies the resident and designated person.

After any behavioral crisis, the Administrator or nurse debriefs staff the same day. They review what happened, what worked and what to change, and update the support plan and, if needed, the assessment (see FRM-03).

If a resident's needs cannot be met without a prohibited practice, the Administrator works with the resident's physician and designated person on additional services or a safe transfer, following POL-16.
The Administrator reviews behavior incidents and rail use quarterly as part of the Quality Management Plan (see POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure no prohibited practice is used, ensure safe-management training within 40 working hours of hire, investigate and report violations.
Use positive interventions, never use prohibited practices, and report behavior incidents and any use of restraint immediately.
Perform the bedside rail assessment, review behavior-related medication changes and advise staff on interventions.
Evaluate behavior changes for medical causes and prescribe medications only for diagnosed conditions.
Review behavior and rail-use data for trends and corrective action.

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff of the Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800), including the special care unit (SCU), if any. The same standard is adopted for any Personal Care Home (Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of residents leaving the residence unsafely, to ensure a prompt, organized search when a resident is missing, and to report unexplained absences as DHS requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies residents at risk of wandering or leaving unsafely and puts individual safety measures in place. Egress routes stay unlocked and unobstructed (55 Pa. Code §§2800.121–2800.124) unless a lock approval is in place for an approved special care unit under 55 Pa. Code §§2800.231–2800.239 (see SCU-01). SCU wandering measures and lock approvals apply in the SCU. Any unexplained absence of a resident is a reportable incident under 55 Pa. Code §2800.16(a)-(b) and is reported to DHS within 24 hours (see POL-01). Staff start a search immediately when a resident is found missing. A resident who leaves the residence for a known, planned purpose is not missing.

definitions.definition: A resident leaving the residence or a secured area without staff knowledge, in a manner that places the resident at risk.
Absence of a resident whose whereabouts are not known and who has not signed out or been accounted for by staff. This is a reportable incident.
Purposeless or disoriented movement that may take a resident into unsafe areas.
Written approval required under the special care unit rules before delayed-egress or other locking arrangements may be used (see SCU-01).
The person named by the resident to be notified of incidents.

procedures: At pre-admission screening and in each assessment, the Administrator or nurse identifies a history of wandering, exit-seeking, confusion or cognitive impairment. The result is recorded in the assessment and support plan (see AR-01 and FRM-03).

For each at-risk resident, the support plan lists specific measures, such as increased checks, scheduled activity, proximity to staff, door alarms or chimes, and a recent photograph and description on file. Staff on every shift review the list.
A current photograph and physical description are kept in a confidential file for each resident at risk. They are updated at least annually and whenever appearance changes.

Staff keep all egress routes unlocked and unobstructed. No door on an exit route is locked, blocked or alarmed in a way that delays exit, unless covered by a written lock approval for the SCU (see SCU-01 and SAF-04).
Residents sign out and in, giving destination and expected return, using the sign-out log. Staff check the log at each shift change and at every meal.
Staff take a headcount at the start of each shift, at every meal, at activities, and after any fire drill or alarm. Any resident who cannot be accounted for is treated as missing.
When a resident is found missing, the staff person calls out an alert and notifies the designee in charge. All available staff stop non-essential tasks.

Staff immediately search the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, outdoor areas, vehicles, and surrounding grounds. Staff check places the resident has been known to go and any approved sign-out information.

Under agency standard, if the resident is not found within 15 minutes of the alert, the designee calls 911 and gives the resident's name, photograph, description, clothing, medical needs and last known location. The designee may call 911 sooner if the resident is high risk, has needs for medications, the weather is dangerous or it is nighttime.
The designee notifies the Administrator immediately and the resident's designated person as soon as the search begins. The designee notes the time of each notification.
One staff person stays at the residence to coordinate, keep the log of search areas and times, and receive calls and police. Residents already accounted for are supervised.

When the resident is found, staff assess for injury and exposure and call 911 as needed. The nurse or physician is contacted. The resident is returned safely and the designated person and police are told.
The Administrator files the reportable incident report with DHS within 24 hours for the unexplained absence (see POL-01). The Administrator also records notification of the designated person.

Within 24 hours of the resident being found, the Administrator and nurse review how the resident left, which measures failed, and what changes are needed. The support plan and, if needed, the assessment are updated (see FRM-03).

If the resident has cognitive impairment and the residence cannot keep the resident safe outside an approved SCU, the Administrator reviews the situation with the resident, designated person and physician under POL-16. SCU placement is possible only if the residence has an approved SCU and the SCU admission requirements are met (see SCU-03).
The Administrator reviews all missing-resident events and near misses quarterly under the Quality Management Plan (see POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain wandering-risk measures, file the 24-hour incident report, review each event and update the plan.
Lead the search, make the 911 call when criteria are met, notify the Administrator and designated person and keep the search log.
Know at-risk residents, keep exits unobstructed, take headcounts, search immediately when alerted.
Identify wandering risk in assessments and assess residents who are found.
Maintain SCU wandering measures and lock approvals.

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Fire Drills
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents, and visitors at the Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800). The same standard is adopted for any Personal Care Home (Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To keep residents safe from fire by maintaining approved fire safety systems, clear exits, trained staff and regular drills, and by documenting all of it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] holds written fire safety approval before licensure and renews it at least every 3 years (55 Pa. Code §2800.14). If approval is withdrawn or restricted, the Administrator notifies DHS orally at once and in writing within 48 hours. After any renovation, the Administrator submits a new approval within 15 days. Egress routes stay unlocked and unobstructed. There are two independent exits per floor. Emergency procedures are posted, and floor diagrams are posted if the residence serves 9 or more residents. A fire-safe area is provided for residents with mobility needs who live above or below grade. The local fire department is notified in writing (55 Pa. Code §§2800.121–2800.124). Each living unit has a smoke detector, tested monthly with a written record and repaired within 48 hours; the residence has an interconnected alarm if 9 or more residents and a monitored connection if 5 or more have mobility needs; extinguishers are provided as required and inspected annually (55 Pa. Code §§2800.130–2800.131). Unannounced fire drills are held monthly, one during sleeping hours every 6 months, plus an annual fire safety expert inspection and drill (55 Pa. Code §2800.132).

definitions.definition: Written approval from the local fire authority or other qualified fire safety official, required before licensure and renewed at least every 3 years.
A person qualified to inspect the residence and conduct the annual drill, who also sets the maximum evacuation time in writing.
A resident's need for assistance or devices to move from one place to another, including evacuation.
A protected area designated for residents who cannot safely use stairs, for those with mobility needs living above or below grade.
The time, set in writing by a fire safety expert, within which all residents must be able to leave the residence.

procedures: Before licensure, the Administrator obtains the written fire safety approval and keeps it on file with the license documents (see PLT-01 and GOV-01). The Administrator calendars its renewal at least every 3 years, with a reminder at least 6 months ahead.
If fire safety approval is withdrawn or restricted, the Administrator notifies DHS orally at once and in writing within 48 hours, and records both notifications.
After any renovation, the Administrator submits a new fire safety approval to DHS within 15 days of the completion of the renovation and files proof of submission.

The Administrator notifies the local fire department in writing of the residence's location, number and mobility needs of residents, and updates the notice when they change. A copy is kept in the fire safety file.

The Administrator or maintenance staff check each shift that egress routes are unlocked and unobstructed. Staff immediately clear any blocked exit route and report any locked door. There are two independent exits on each floor.

Emergency procedures are posted in each area where residents live or gather. If 9 or more residents are served, evacuation floor diagrams are posted on each floor, showing exits, routes and fire-safe areas.

Residents with mobility needs who live above or below grade are housed in line with the fire-safe area plan. The Administrator documents the fire-safe area and evacuation method on the evacuation plan and the resident's assessment.

Maintenance staff test the smoke detector in each living unit monthly and record the date, unit, result and initials. Any defective detector is repaired or replaced within 48 hours, and until then staff take interim safety steps (see POL-11).

The residence's interconnected smoke alarm system (9 or more residents) and monitored connection (5 or more residents with mobility needs) are tested at the intervals required by the system installer and fire safety expert. Results are recorded.

Fire extinguishers are provided as follows: a 2-A extinguisher on each floor and for every 3,000 square feet, and a 2A-10BC in the kitchen. A qualified person inspects all extinguishers annually. The tag date and inspection record are kept.

The Administrator conducts an unannounced fire drill every month. Drills are varied by day of the week, time of day and exit used, and staff do not announce them in advance. One drill every 6 months is held during resident sleeping hours.
Once a year, a fire safety expert inspects the residence and conducts or oversees an evacuation drill. The expert sets in writing the maximum time within which residents must evacuate.

During each drill, staff sound the alarm, assist residents using the posted plan, close doors, account for every resident by headcount, and time the evacuation. If the time set by the fire safety expert is not met, the Administrator reviews the cause, retrains staff and holds another drill soon.
For each drill the Administrator or designee completes a written record showing date, time, exit used, number of residents and staff, evacuation time, problems and corrective action (see FRM-04).
New staff are trained on the fire plan, extinguisher use and evacuation during orientation, and annually thereafter (see TRN-01). Staff also learn each resident's evacuation needs.

In a real fire or alarm, staff follow the posted procedure: rescue residents in immediate danger, sound the alarm, call 911, close doors, evacuate, headcount, and meet at [ASSEMBLY POINT]. The Administrator then reports the fire as a reportable incident (see POL-01) and adjusts the plan (see POL-09).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain fire safety approval and DHS notifications, conduct drills, ensure testing and inspections are done and records kept.
Test smoke detectors monthly, repair within 48 hours, check exits and extinguishers.
Know evacuation plans, keep exits clear, take part in drills and evacuate residents.

responsibilities.role: Fire safety expert / local fire official

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents, volunteers and visitors at the Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800). The same standard is adopted for any Personal Care Home (Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents and staff, to ensure each resident's tuberculosis (TB) test is documented, to report outbreaks, and to keep the residence sanitary and free of pests.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows standard precautions and maintains a sanitary environment. Each resident has a TB test within 2 years before admission, or within 15 days of admission, recorded in the resident's medical evaluation on the DHS form (55 Pa. Code §2800.141, see FRM-02). The evaluation is repeated at least annually and when the resident's medical condition changes. An outbreak is a reportable incident under 55 Pa. Code §2800.16(a)-(b) and is reported to DHS as POL-01 requires. The residence stays sanitary, with no insect or rodent infestation. Trash is removed at least weekly and kept in covered receptacles (55 Pa. Code §2800.85). Where a residence serving 9 or more residents is on a private sewer system, written sewage-system approval is on file (see SEW-01). Staff who may be exposed to blood or other potentially infectious materials are protected under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030.

definitions.definition: Basic infection control practices used with all residents, including hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, safe handling of sharps, respiratory hygiene and cleaning of equipment and surfaces.

An unusual increase of an infectious illness among residents or staff, such as two or more linked cases of gastrointestinal or respiratory illness, as defined by the Pennsylvania Department of Health. An outbreak is a reportable incident.
Disease-causing microorganisms in human blood, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, covered by 29 CFR 1910.1030.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin, or needlestick contact with blood or other potentially infectious material while on duty.
A tuberculosis screening test recorded on the resident's medical evaluation, done within 2 years before admission or within 15 days of admission.

procedures: Before or at admission, the Administrator obtains the resident's medical evaluation on the DHS form, completed by a physician, physician assistant or certified registered nurse practitioner, with the TB test result. If the TB test is not within 2 years before admission, it is completed within 15 days of admission (see FRM-02 and AR-01).

If the TB test is positive or the resident has symptoms of active TB, the Administrator or nurse follows the physician's orders and Department of Health guidance on further evaluation and any needed isolation or precautions, and records the actions taken.
The medical evaluation is repeated at least every year and when the resident's medical condition changes. The Administrator tracks the due dates.
The Administrator adopts a written infection control and exposure control plan that identifies tasks with exposure risk. The plan is reviewed annually (see POL-03).

New staff are trained on standard precautions, hand hygiene, glove use, handling sharps and soiled linen, and exposure response before they provide care, and annually after that. Training is documented (see TRN-01 and PLAN-01).

At no cost to staff, the Administrator makes available the hepatitis B vaccination series and the protective equipment (gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection) required by 29 CFR 1910.1030. Staff who decline sign a declination form.

Staff wash or sanitize hands before and after resident contact, before meal preparation and medication passes, and after using the toilet or handling soiled items. Gloves are worn for contact with blood, body fluids or non-intact skin and are changed between residents.

Used needles and lancets, if any, go into labeled puncture-resistant containers at the point of use. Contaminated laundry is handled with gloves, bagged where it is used and washed separately. Regulated waste is disposed of as the law requires.

After an exposure incident, the staff person washes the area right away, reports to the Administrator or designee, and is sent for medical evaluation and follow-up. The Administrator records the incident, keeps the record confidential and reviews how to prevent it.

Staff or residents with signs of contagious illness, such as vomiting, diarrhea, fever with cough or an unexplained rash, are assessed by the nurse or physician. Staff excluded from work are kept off duty until the physician or health official clears them. Ill residents are cared for in their living unit, with precautions, as directed by the nurse or physician.

Staff keep an illness line list with names, onset dates, symptoms and location. If two or more linked cases occur, the Administrator treats it as a possible outbreak, tells the physician and the Department of Health as required by law, and increases cleaning and precautions.
The Administrator reports an outbreak to DHS as a reportable incident within the time stated in POL-01, and notifies residents' designated persons. The report and follow-up are logged.

Housekeeping staff clean and disinfect bathrooms, high-touch surfaces and shared equipment daily and as needed, using products listed for healthcare use and following label directions. Resident rooms are cleaned on a set schedule and when soiled.
Staff remove trash from the residence at least weekly, and more often as needed, and keep trash in covered receptacles. Dumpsters and trash areas are kept clean and away from food areas.

The Administrator contracts with a licensed pest control service as needed and checks monthly for signs of insects or rodents. If any are found, the Administrator has them treated immediately, records the treatment and confirms the problem is resolved.

If the residence serves 9 or more residents and uses a private sewer system, the Administrator keeps the written sewage-system approval on file and has any sewage backup repaired immediately (see SEW-01).
Resident vaccinations and immunization offers (such as influenza and pneumonia) are offered through the resident's physician and recorded. Resident refusals are recorded.
The Administrator reviews infection data, exposure incidents and sanitation findings each quarter in the Quality Management Plan (see POL-03).

policies.title: Food Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: All staff involved in food service, nursing and care, and all residents of the Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800). The same standard is adopted for any Personal Care Home (Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive safe, nutritious meals and snacks that meet USDA allowances and prescribed diets, with safe food storage, adequate dining space and prompt action when a resident refuses food or drink.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] serves three meals daily that meet USDA allowances, with an alternative item offered at each meal, plus snacks (55 Pa. Code §§2800.161–2800.164). The maximum gap between meals is 6 hours, and the maximum overnight gap between the evening meal and breakfast is 15 hours. One-week menus are posted. Prescribed diets are followed. A dietitian, on staff or under contract, plans and reviews therapeutic diets (55 Pa. Code §2800.60). Refrigerated food is kept at or below 40°F and frozen food at or below 0°F, with thermometers in each unit, and common dining space is provided at 15 square feet per person (55 Pa. Code §§2800.103–2800.105). Staff never withhold food or drink as punishment or force a resident to eat. If a resident refuses food or drink for 24 hours, the physician and the designated person are notified. Food service staff hours are in addition to the minimum direct care staffing, as 55 Pa. Code §2800.60 requires.

definitions.definition: The nutritional recommendations of the U.S. Department of Agriculture that meals must meet, in the amounts required by regulation.
A diet ordered by a physician, physician assistant or CRNP for a medical condition, such as diabetic, low sodium, renal, texture-modified or thickened-liquid diets.
A substitute food or beverage offered to a resident who does not want the main menu item at a meal.
A licensed dietitian-nutritionist employed or contracted by [AGENCY NAME] to plan menus and diets and advise staff (see CON-01).
The person the resident has named to be notified of changes in condition.

procedures: The Administrator employs or contracts with a dietitian and lists the dietitian on the consultant list (see CON-01). The dietitian approves the menu cycle and therapeutic diet procedures and reviews them at least annually.
The cook or food service lead writes menus at least one week ahead, based on USDA allowances, resident preferences and the dietitian's guidance. Each meal lists an alternative item.
One-week menus are posted where residents can see them in the dining area. If a substitution is needed, it is of equal nutritional value and written on the posted menu.

Three meals are served daily at set times, and the schedule is posted. Between-meal snacks and beverages are offered and available, and the gap rules are met: no more than 6 hours between meals and no more than 15 hours overnight. Staff plan an evening snack so that the overnight gap does not exceed 15 hours.

At admission, the nurse or Administrator records each resident's diet order, food allergies, swallowing or chewing problems and preferences from the medical evaluation and assessment (see FRM-02 and FRM-03). This information is shared with kitchen staff and posted in the kitchen away from public view.

When a physician or other prescriber orders a therapeutic diet, the nurse gives the written order to the cook, the dietitian reviews it, and the diet begins at the next meal. Staff prepare and serve it as prescribed, including texture and liquid thickness.
Before each meal, the cook and care staff check each tray or plate against the diet list. Staff who serve food know which residents need special diets, assistance or supervision at meals.
Staff provide meal assistance and adaptive equipment as shown in the support plan and stay with residents who are at risk of choking.
Common dining space is provided at 15 square feet per person. The Administrator verifies the space against the number of residents who dine at one seating, and adds seatings if needed (see PLT-01).

Kitchen staff check refrigerator and freezer thermometers at least daily and record the temperatures. Refrigerated food must be at or below 40°F and frozen food at or below 0°F. If a unit is out of range, the cook notifies the Administrator, moves food, discards unsafe items and arranges repair.

Food is labeled and dated, stored off the floor, kept covered, and raw foods are stored below ready-to-eat foods. Staff follow safe handwashing, cooking and cooling practices. Food service staff with illness do not handle food.
Dietitian visits: the dietitian reviews each resident with a therapeutic diet, weight loss or other nutrition risk at least [FREQUENCY] and records recommendations. The nurse carries out the orders.

Staff weigh each resident monthly, or more often if ordered, and report significant weight change to the nurse. The nurse notifies the physician and the dietitian and updates the support plan (see HC-01).

Staff never withhold food or drink for any reason, such as punishment or convenience, and never force a resident to eat or drink. Staff respect resident choices and offer alternatives, changed timing or assistance.

If a resident refuses food or drink, staff record each refusal. When a resident refuses food or drink for 24 hours, the designee notifies the physician and the designated person that day, records the call, and follows medical direction (see HC-01).

Staffing: the Administrator schedules enough food service hours in addition to direct care hours so that meals are prepared, served and cleaned up without drawing direct care staff from residents (see STF-01 and STF-02).
The Administrator reviews resident satisfaction with meals, menu compliance, diet errors and temperature logs each quarter in the Quality Management Plan (see POL-03).

policies.title: Activities, Transportation, Housekeeping and Laundry
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800). The same standards are adopted as the agency's standard for any Personal Care Home (55 Pa. Code Ch. 2600) operated by [AGENCY NAME]. All residents and all staff who plan activities, drive, clean or handle laundry.
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives the daily living services [AGENCY NAME] has promised in its Description of Services: a daily activities program, weekly transportation, a clean and pest-free home, and laundry service. These are provided on the schedules and under the safety conditions Pennsylvania regulations require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a daily activities program, transportation, housekeeping and laundry services to all residents as part of the services listed in 55 Pa. Code §2800.220(b) and in our written Description of Services (55 Pa. Code §§2800.220–2800.223). (1) ACTIVITIES: A daily activities program is a required service. Activities are planned with resident input, match residents' interests and abilities, and include cognitive support for residents who need it. Participation is voluntary. (2) TRANSPORTATION: [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges transportation at least weekly (55 Pa. Code §2800.171). Drivers are at least 18 years old and hold a valid driver's license. Each vehicle used for residents carries a first aid kit and has current registration, insurance and inspection records on file. If [AGENCY NAME] supplies vehicles, at least one is wheelchair-accessible. Pickups occur within 15 minutes of the scheduled time. (3) HOUSEKEEPING AND SANITATION: The residence is kept clean and sanitary and free of insect and rodent infestation. Trash is kept in covered receptacles and removed at least weekly (55 Pa. Code §2800.85). Where the residence serves 9 or more residents on a private sewer system, written sewage-system approval is kept on file (see SEW-01). (4) LAUNDRY AND LINENS: Bed linens are changed at least weekly, and residents' personal clothing is returned within 24 hours (55 Pa. Code §§2800.103–2800.105). Laundry service is provided free of charge to residents who receive SSI. (5) FOOD SAFETY AND DINING SPACE: Food storage temperatures are monitored (refrigerated at or below 40°F, frozen at or below 0°F, with thermometers in each unit). Common dining space provides at least 15 square feet per person (see DL-01). This policy has no checklist items assigned to it.

definitions.definition: A written, scheduled set of social, recreational, physical, cognitive, spiritual and community activities offered every day and based on resident interests and abilities.
Services and activities that help residents with memory, orientation and thinking needs maintain function and engagement, as listed in the Description of Services.
Garments and personal items owned by the resident that [AGENCY NAME] launders for the resident, as distinct from facility-owned bed and bath linens.
A resident who receives Supplemental Security Income, with or without a state supplement, as verified at admission or when payer status changes.
The time communicated to the resident or representative for a trip or appointment. The vehicle must arrive within 15 minutes of it.

procedures: ACTIVITIES: Within 30 days of admission, the Activities Coordinator interviews each resident (and representative if appropriate) about interests, routines, abilities, cultural and spiritual preferences, and records them on the resident's activity preference sheet.

The Activities Coordinator prepares a written monthly activities calendar that includes activities every day, drawing on resident preferences and including physical, social, cognitive, creative and community-based options. The Administrator approves it before the start of the month.

The calendar is posted in a common area and in large print, and a copy is given to each resident on request. Staff remind residents with cognitive or sensory impairments of activities in a way they can understand.

Activities are adapted for residents with mobility, vision, hearing or cognitive needs, and individual or in-room activities are offered to residents who cannot or do not wish to join groups. Staff on duty support participation.

The Activities Coordinator keeps a daily attendance record showing the activity held, the date, and the residents who took part. Residents who decline are recorded as declined, not as absent. The Activities Coordinator reviews participation monthly and revises the calendar based on resident feedback, including feedback from resident meetings.

TRANSPORTATION: Before first use, the Administrator verifies that each driver (staff or contracted) is at least 18 years old and holds a valid driver's license. A copy of the license is kept in the driver's personnel file, and license status is re-checked at least annually and after any reported incident.

The Administrator keeps a transportation file for each vehicle used to transport residents. It contains registration, proof of insurance and current inspection records, and it is checked quarterly for expiration dates.

Every vehicle carries a stocked first aid kit. The driver checks the kit before each trip, and the Administrator replaces missing or expired items at the monthly vehicle check. If [AGENCY NAME] supplies vehicles, at least one is wheelchair-accessible and its lift or ramp and securement devices are inspected before use.

The Transportation Coordinator publishes a weekly transportation schedule (for example, scheduled shopping, medical or community outings) and takes individual appointment requests at [PHONE]. Residents are told the pickup time in advance.

Drivers arrive within 15 minutes of the scheduled pickup time. If a delay will exceed 15 minutes, staff notify the resident immediately and the Transportation Coordinator arranges a backup vehicle or reschedules. Each late pickup is recorded on the trip log with the cause.

Staff accompany residents who need assistance or supervision on trips, and the driver confirms that every resident is seated, buckled and safely returned. Any accident or injury during transport is reported to the Administrator immediately and handled under POL-01 (Reportable Incidents).

The Transportation Coordinator keeps a trip log showing date, driver, vehicle, riders, destination, scheduled and actual pickup times, and any incident. Charges, if any, are disclosed in the resident contract (FRM-01 and RR-01).

HOUSEKEEPING: Housekeeping staff follow a written cleaning schedule covering resident units, bathrooms, common areas, the kitchen and dining area, and storage areas. The schedule is signed off daily, and the Administrator spot-checks at least weekly.

Trash is kept in covered receptacles and removed from the residence at least weekly (more often, such as daily, from kitchens, bathrooms and units with soiled items). Staff report signs of insects or rodents to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator arranges licensed pest control, and the service date and treatment are recorded in the pest-control log.

Kitchen staff record refrigerator and freezer temperatures daily (refrigerated at or below 40°F, frozen at or below 0°F), using thermometers in each unit. Out-of-range readings are corrected and food safety is assessed as set out in DL-01, which also covers dining room space of 15 square feet per person. The Administrator checks the sewage-system approval for any private system serving 9 or more residents, as described in SEW-01.

LAUNDRY: Laundry staff change bed linens at least weekly and sooner when soiled. Each change is signed off on the weekly linen record. Residents' personal clothing is laundered, labeled, and returned within 24 hours of collection, and the return is tracked on the laundry log.

At admission and whenever a resident's payer status changes, the Business Office verifies whether the resident receives SSI. Laundry service is provided to SSI residents at no charge, and no laundry fee is billed to them. Other laundry charges, if any, are disclosed in the resident contract. Soiled or infectious linen is handled according to SAF-05.

Residents and representatives may raise concerns about activities, transportation, housekeeping or laundry with any staff member or the Administrator, or through POL-07. The Administrator reviews these concerns and the logs described above quarterly and reports trends to the Quality Management Plan (POL-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the monthly activities calendar, verifies driver licenses and vehicle records, oversees housekeeping, pest control and laundry compliance, and reviews logs and complaints quarterly.
Interviews residents, prepares and posts the daily activities calendar, adapts activities, records attendance, and reports participation trends.
Publishes the weekly transportation schedule, assigns qualified drivers and vehicles, manages late pickups, and keeps trip logs.
Hold a valid license, are at least 18, inspect the first aid kit and vehicle before trips, pick up residents within 15 minutes of schedule, and report any incident immediately.
Complete the cleaning schedule, remove trash at least weekly in covered receptacles, change linens at least weekly, return clothing within 24 hours, and report pests.
Record refrigerator and freezer temperatures daily and keep dining and kitchen areas sanitary.
Verifies SSI status and ensures no laundry charge is billed to SSI residents.

official.notes: Each checklist is submitted to the BHSL headquarters office before the initial inspection of a new facility, or of a sale or change of legal entity, is scheduled. The checklist says BHSL may request additional materials, or the materials in a different order than listed. The reviewer therefore expects the packet to follow the checklist's own numbering (1-18, with lettered sub-items), with each policy labelled by item number and regulation cite (e.g., '8(a) Reportable Incidents and Conditions Policy – § 2800.16(b)'). The ALR (Ch. 2800) and PCH (Ch. 2600) checklists are separate; a facility licensed as an ALR submits the ALR version and a PCH submits the PCH version. 'doc': 0 is the ALR checklist and 'doc': 1 is the PCH checklist. Items I left out of required_items as application or evidence paperwork, not policy content: 1 (administrator credentials), 2 (the criminal history clearances themselves), 7 (floor plans, elevator certificate, SCU/SDCU site evidence), 9(a) (written SCU/SDCU request), and 11-18. Item 1 (administrator qualifications) is also omitted from required_items, and it is the only omitted item that is partly staffing content. Item 10 is a list of 'forms' (contract, rights poster, fire drill record, assessment and support plan forms, MAR). I kept those as operating documents, not application forms. Drop them if you want strictly written policies. Special Care Unit / Secured Dementia Care Unit items and swimming pool, firearms and smoking policies apply only if applicable. The checklist for the Certificate of Compliance application (hs633-checklist.pdf) covers non-policy paperwork such as fees, occupancy permit and civil rights form. I did not use it. Those fees are not stated consistently across sources (for example, per-bed amounts), so check the current fee schedule. The Ch. 2800 and Ch. 2600 regulation sections cited in brackets are the authority for the content of each policy. I could not open the pacodeandbulletin.gov pages, so each policy's required contents come from the regulation text, which I did not read.
